Abstract:
Micro-opto-electro-mechanical systems (MOEMS) based mirrors with a suitable actuation range are often used for optical beam scanning applications. While several MOEMS scanners have been reported, they often have limitations with respect to their range of motion, field of view, mass, size and fabrication cost. In this work, we present a rotary micro-polygon scanner based on an electrostatic variable capacitance micromotor for laser beam steering applications. The miniaturized scanner consists of a hollow micro-polyhedron mirror with a base radius of <inline-formula> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$200 {\mu }\text{m}$ </tex-math></inline-formula> and a height of <inline-formula> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$400 {\mu }\text{m}$ </tex-math></inline-formula>. It is mounted on the rotor of a variable capacitance micromotor using an epoxy-based adhesive. The rotor has a diameter of <inline-formula> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$600 {\mu }\text{m}$ </tex-math></inline-formula> and is <inline-formula> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$2.5 {\mu }\text{m}$ </tex-math></inline-formula> thick. The micromotor was fabricated using a commercial three-layer polysilicon surface micro-machining process (PolyMUMPs) and the micro-polyhedrons were fabricated using a commercial bulk micro-machining process (PiezeoMUMPs). After fabrication of the components, the micro-scanner was assembled and operated under atmospheric conditions using a three-phase square wave excitation ranging from 0 V to 200 V and achieved rotational speeds of up to 2100 rpm. An optical laser beam with a wavelength of 632 nm was reflected off the sidewall of the rotating micro-polyhedron, achieving an experimentally measured scanning angular range of 57.88°, an angular scan rate of 220 radians per second and a scan speed of 25,200 lines per minute or 420 lines per second with a 12 sided micro-mirror. The ratio of the output power over the input optical power is measured over a scanning range of 22°, which is limited by the size of the photo-detector, yielding a ratio spanning from 0.18 to 0.22. This rotary micro-scanner can provide high scanning speeds and a wide scanning field of view with a footprint of 1.25 mm<sup>2</sup> and a thickness of 0.83 mm, which is suitable to implement chip-level high-performance micro-beam steering systems for various applications. Abstract:
A novel visual 3D reconstruction system, composed of a two-axis galvanometer scanner, a camera with a lens, and a set of control units, is introduced in this paper. By changing the mirror angles of the galvanometer scanner fixed in front of the camera, the boresight of the camera can be quickly adjusted. With the variable boresight, the camera can serve as a virtual multi-ocular system (VMOS), which captures the object at different perspectives. The working mechanism with a definite physical meaning is presented. A simple and efficient method for calibrating the intrinsic and extrinsic parameters of the VMOS is presented. The applicability of the proposed system for 3D reconstruction is investigated. Owing to the multiple virtual poses of the camera, the VMOS can provide stronger constraints in the object pose estimation than an ordinary perspective camera does. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed VMOS is able to achieve 3D reconstruction performance competitive with that of a conventional stereovision system with a much more concise hardware configuration.

Include these steps: unpacking deliveries, sawing bar stock, CNC mill loading/unloading (including 34.7kg plate), CNC lathe loading/unloading, deburring, ultrasonic washing, measuring/inspection, kitting parts, O-ring installation (face glands, dovetail grooves, rod glands with ring loaders/rollers/mandrels), M3-M6 stainless screw driving (nutrunner + angle head), dowel pins, helical inserts, bearings, ball screw and linear rail, cartridge heaters and thermocouples, optics (galvo scan head, f-theta lens M85 thread), cable/hose/fiber routing, TIG welding thin-wall 316L, bore gauge reading, threading small fittings with tubes, felt-and-PTFE bore seal, final integration (84kg process module). For each, note whether the user's current assignment is correct or should be changed."}
function.name: create_artifact

messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-00)

| Step | Cobot Feasibility | Key Challenges | Recommended Assignment |
|---|---|---|---|
| Unpacking deliveries | Low | Unknown box geometry, straps and film, clutter, hidden or fragile contents, variable grasp points, and pose estimation; robots remain sensitive to object and pose variation (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000047) | **Shared — change plan.** Person opens packages and resolves exceptions; robots move standardized totes and known parts to inspection or kitting stations. |
| Sawing bar stock | Medium | Requires a guarded automatic saw, stock feeder, positive stops, chip control, and safe machine interface; loose long stock is awkward for a mobile cobot. | **Shared — change plan.** Person stages long/heavy stock and sets the first cut; robot can load short standardized blanks and unload cut pieces after validation. |
| CNC mill loading/unloading, ordinary parts | High | Chips or coolant on jaws and datums, part orientation, door/chuck interlocks, tool clearance, and verification that the workpiece is fully seated; mobile tending remains largely prototype-level when the environment is not tightly structured (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000033, pqac-00000038) | **Robot with human setup — retain plan.** Automate repeat loads only after CAM, first article, fixture setup, and a proven cleaning/seating routine. |
| CNC mill loading/unloading, 34.7 kg plate | Not Feasible | Plate exceeds the two arms’ combined nominal 25 kg payload before grippers, vacuum tooling, load sharing uncertainty, dynamics, and safety margin; coordinated mobile bases are not a certified lifting device. | **Human with rated vacuum lifter — retain plan.** Do not attempt dual-arm lifting; use a hoist, lifter, or higher-payload industrial robot. |
| CNC lathe loading/unloading | High | Chuck cleanliness, jaw engagement, bar protrusion, part ejection, slippery coolant-covered parts, and confirmation of clamp state. | **Robot with human setup — retain plan.** Use chuck confirmation, force-monitored insertion, part-present sensing, and periodic human inspection. |
| Deburring | Medium | Burr location and size vary; compliant tooling can miss edges or alter critical sealing surfaces, threads, and precision bores. Force-based processes add tooling and commissioning complexity (pqac-00000051) | **Shared — change plan.** Robot only repeatable external edges with compliant tools; person handles one-off internal features, sealing lands, threads, and final tactile inspection. |
| Ultrasonic washing | High | Basket loading, liquid carryover, drying, contamination control, and chemical exposure; process must be enclosed and interlocked. | **Robot — retain plan.** Use standardized perforated baskets, drip dwell, rinse/dry stations, and presence checks. |
| Measuring and inspection with machine-readable instruments | Medium | Reliable datum seating, probe access, calibration, temperature, part identification, and interpreting unexpected results; perception and sensor robustness remain deployment barriers (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000047) | **Shared — change plan.** Robot can operate digital calipers, height probes, vision, or a gauging fixture; person owns the inspection plan, calibration, ambiguous readings, and first-article disposition. |
| Kitting parts onto the long table | High | Long-table reach requires multiple docks; kit verification, small-part singulation, and preventing wrong-part placement. Fiducial or station calibration can reduce mobile-position error substantially, but task-level local sensing remains necessary (pqac-00000034, pqac-00000035) | **Robot — retain plan.** Use compartmented trays, barcodes or vision, AprilTag registration, and a weight or vision completeness check. |
| FKM O-rings in open face glands | Medium | Elastomer variability, lubrication, stretch control, twist, incomplete seating, and weak visual contrast. | **Robot after development — retain only conditionally.** Dedicated expanding mandrel or ring-loader plus 360° post-install inspection is credible; keep a person for exceptions and leak-critical acceptance. |
| FKM O-rings in half-dovetail grooves | Low | The ring must be stretched, rolled under the retaining lip, and seated without shaving or twist; force alone does not prove correct circumferential seating. | **Shared — change plan.** Treat as a development task, not assumed production capability; robot may install with a custom roller, but require human inspection or validated full-circumference machine vision. |
| FKM O-rings in internal rod-gland grooves | Low | Occluded groove, restricted tool access, risk of cutting, twist or partial seating, and difficult inspection. | **Human initially — change plan.** Automate only after a dedicated insertion cartridge or mandrel and borescope inspection demonstrate high reliability on representative glands. |
| M3–M6 stainless screws with straight nutrunner | High | Screw presentation, bit engagement, hole localization, stainless galling, cross-threading, torque scatter, and dropped screws. Torque–angle windows and torque-rate monitoring detect abnormal tightening, but require teaching and validation; reported general fault-recognition results are about 90–97%, not zero-defect assurance (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000039, pqac-00000040) | **Robot — retain plan.** Use captive or vacuum-fed screws, low-speed thread start, axial compliance, reverse-to-find-thread, torque–angle trace storage, lubrication or approved anti-seize, and human review of rejects. |
| M3–M6 stainless screws with angle-head nutrunner | Medium | Restricted access, reaction torque, tool-body collision, visibility, bit alignment, and reduced ability to recover from a bad start. | **Shared — change plan.** Automate only accessible, well-fixtured locations; redesign for straight access where possible and leave obstructed fasteners to a person. |
| Dowel pins | High | Tight alignment, chamfer condition, incorrect pin length, excessive insertion force, and false seating. Force/torque search and compliant peg-in-hole methods are established for structured assembly (pqac-00000025) | **Robot — retain plan.** Use force-limited spiral search and verify final depth plus force–displacement signature. Use a press for true interference fits. |
| Helical inserts | Medium | Tang pickup, insert compression, pitch following, cross-threading, depth control, and tang break/removal verification. | **Shared — change plan.** Robot can install repetitive inserts with a dedicated driver; person verifies threads, depth, tang removal, and repairs failures. |
| Bearings | Medium | Must press on the correct race, maintain squareness, control force, protect cleanliness, and distinguish seating from jamming. | **Shared — change plan.** Robot transfers and starts bearings; a guided instrumented press performs insertion and records force–displacement. Person handles high-value or ambiguous fits. |
| Ball screw and linear rail | Medium | Long flexible components, contamination, alignment, rail straightness, staged tightening, preload, and risk of damaging ball circuits or wipers. | **Shared — change plan.** Robots can place rails and drive accessible screws in sequence; person aligns, indicates, checks smoothness/preload, and handles the ball screw installation. |
| Cartridge heaters and thermocouples | Medium | Fragile leads, bore fit, thermal compound, bend-radius control, retention, polarity/type identification, and subsequent cable routing. | **Shared — change plan.** Robot may insert rigid cartridges and probes into clean, chamfered bores; person routes and terminates leads and verifies continuity and insulation. |
| Optics: galvo scan head placement | Medium | Cleanliness, mass properties, connector protection, precision datums, optical alignment, and calibration; scanner performance depends on machine-specific assembly and optical errors (pqac-00000045) | **Shared — change plan.** Robot may transfer and bolt a capped scan head onto kinematic datums; person performs cleanliness inspection, optical alignment, calibration, and acceptance. |
| Optics: f-theta lens on M85 thread | Low | Expensive fragile optic, contamination, fine-thread start, large threaded diameter, uncertain starting phase, cross-threading, galling or binding, and torque without damaging the lens. | **Human — change plan.** Install in a clean area with purpose-made support and torque method; robotic installation is unjustified for one unit unless the lens cartridge is redesigned with lead-ins and error-proofing. |
| Cable, hose, and fibre routing | Low | Deformable objects have high configuration uncertainty, occlusion, snagging, connector handling, bend-radius and tension constraints. Robots can route known cables through known clips with tactile sensing, but general 3-D routing remains an open problem (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021) | **Human — retain plan.** Robots may preform, present, or clip simple harness segments, but a person should route the one-off hoses, fibres, and cables. |
| TIG welding thin-wall 316L tube to flanges | Low | Joint fit-up, purge quality, distortion, arc-length and heat-input control, seam tracking, shielding, fume extraction, welding qualification, and fire hazards. In HMLV practice, programming burden can make even technically suitable cobot welding uneconomic (pqac-00000032) | **Skilled human welder — retain plan.** A one-off qualified weld is not a sensible first cobot-welding application. |
| Reading bore gauges and height gauges | Medium | Correct rocking or sweeping technique, consistent contact force, datum cleanliness, calibration, and interpretation of unstable readings. | **Human for present build — retain plan.** Automation is possible with digital gauges and dedicated fixtures, but commissioning it for one machine is unlikely to repay the effort. |
| Threading small fittings with tubes attached | Low | Flexible tube reaction, uncertain starting phase, cross-threading, wrench access, sealant control, tube twist, and inability to distinguish galling from normal tightening reliably. | **Human — retain plan.** Robot may hold or present components, but a person should start threads, control tube orientation, and make the final connection. |
| Felt-and-PTFE bore seal | Low | Soft, easily creased or damaged layers, hidden seating, friction, overlapping or split-joint control, and poor force signature. | **Human — retain plan.** Purpose-built tooling could automate a repeated design, but one-off commissioning and inspection are disproportionate. |
| Final integration: 84 kg process module onto tray | Not Feasible | Far beyond combined cobot payload; suspended-load, crush, pinch, alignment, and mobile-base stability hazards. | **Person directing a rated hoist — retain plan.** Robots may observe fiducials or guide alignment only if they never support or enter beneath the suspended load. |


*Table: Step-by-step assessment of which machining and assembly operations fit present-day cobots and where human work or task redesign remains necessary. The recommendations also identify where the proposed allocation should be retained or changed.*

function.arguments: {"artifact_type": "table", "description": "Create a table of the key failure modes for the proposed mobile manipulator cell, with columns: Failure Mode, Severity (High/Medium/Low), Detection Method, Mitigation Strategy. Include these failure modes: 1) AMR docking/positioning error, 2) Chips or coolant contaminating fixtures/parts, 3) Part pose error (wrong orientation in gripper or fixture), 4) Cross-threading of stainless screws, 5) Galling of stainless steel fasteners, 6) Dropped parts, 7) O-ring twist or incomplete seating, 8) Fixture/vise seating failure, 9) Tool breakage during machining, 10) Collision between robot and CNC machine, 11) Optics contamination, 12) Wrong part picked or assembled."}
function.name: create_artifact

messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-01)

| Failure Mode | Severity (High/Medium/Low) | Detection Method | Mitigation Strategy |
|---|---|---|---|
| AMR docking or station-positioning error | High | Verify the AprilTag pose, reprojection residual, tag count and station transform before every manipulation; probe three or more fixed station datums with the wrist tool; reject transforms outside a validated covariance envelope. SLAM-only errors of 50–100 mm have been reported, versus ≤10 mm with ARTags; calibrated station referencing has achieved approximately ±0.12 mm in a structured example (pqac-00000034, pqac-00000035). | Use positive mechanical docking or wheel brakes, guarded fiducials, redundant tags, local datum probing and a station-specific transform—not AMR pose alone. Permit only slow free-space motion until registration passes; abort and redock on disagreement between vision and touch-off results. |
| Chips or coolant contaminating fixtures or parts | High | Dedicated close-up vision of jaws and datums; air-pressure/flow monitoring; force–displacement signature during seating; fixture gap, vacuum or part-present sensors; inspect the first part after every intervention. | Add chip-resistant jaws and datum geometry, directed air blast or wash/dry cycles, coolant-compatible grippers and protected optics. Require a clean–inspect–load–seat–verify sequence; route exceptions to a person rather than repeating a forceful insertion. |
| Part pose error in the gripper or fixture | High | Wrist-camera pose estimate immediately after pickup and again before insertion; gripper-width or jaw-position check; mass/vacuum confirmation; force-controlled guarded approach. Robotic deployment remains sensitive to object and pose variation, and force/torque data should be interpreted relative to part geometry (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000045). | Use keyed nests, asymmetrical grasp features, hard stops, poka-yoke fixtures and constrained part presentation. Regrasp or reject if independent vision and gripper-state estimates disagree; never compensate for a large pose error by forcing the part into place. |
| Cross-threading of stainless screws | High | Record torque versus angle from initial engagement onward; flag early torque rise, insufficient free-run angle, abnormal torque rate or a trace outside the taught envelope. General screwdriving-fault classifiers report roughly 90–97% recognition, but this is not zero-defect assurance (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000040). | Use chamfered holes, axial compliance, low-speed thread start and a reverse rotation to locate the thread lead. Stop at a low snug-torque threshold, back out and retry only once; quarantine repeated failures for manual thread inspection. |
| Galling of stainless-steel fasteners | High | Detect a rapid or irregular torque increase before expected seating angle, stick–slip in the torque trace, abnormal tool current or heat, and failure to back out at low reverse torque. Torque-only inference is uncertain because friction can cause errors approaching 50% (pqac-00000008). | Use compatible fastener grades/coatings, approved anti-seize or pre-applied lubricant, clean threads and slow driving speed. Avoid prevailing-torque hardware unless validated; define conservative torque–angle windows and discard—not reuse—any suspect screw or threaded component. |
| Dropped part or screw | High | Gripper-position, vacuum and pressure switches; load or wrist-force check after pickup; downward-looking vision over the transfer path; tray weight or receiving-nest part-present sensor. Threaded-part insertion experiments show that a poorly aligned part can hang insecurely and fall on release (pqac-00000025). | Use fail-safe normally closed gripping where practical, dual vacuum channels with check valves, retained or captive screws, minimum safe grip margins and low transfer heights. Provide catch trays and exclusion zones; stop the cell and reconcile inventory after every detected drop. |
| O-ring twist, cut or incomplete seating | High | Full-circumference machine vision or borescope inspection for continuity, protrusion and surface damage; compare installation force and tool travel with validated envelopes; perform leak or pressure-decay testing after closure. Force alone cannot prove untwisted seating in an occluded groove. | Control lubrication, ring orientation, stretch and insertion speed; use dedicated expanding mandrels, rollers or installation cartridges with rounded edges. Require validated automated inspection for open glands and human borescope inspection for half-dovetail or internal rod glands until process capability is demonstrated. |
| Fixture or vise seating failure | High | Verify clamp-state signal and commanded pressure; measure part-to-datum gap with displacement, proximity or vision sensing; compare insertion force–travel and work-offset probing with a golden cycle; monitor the first machining cut for anomalous load. | Clean and inspect datums before every load; use chip-shedding fixture geometry, positive locating pins, controlled clamping and redundant part-present sensing. Do not start the CNC from the clamp signal alone; require independent seating confirmation. |
| Tool breakage or severe wear during machining | High | CNC spindle-load and axis-current limits, acoustic-emission or vibration monitoring, tool-length probing after critical operations, in-process probing and dimensional checks; monitor coolant flow and machine alarms. | Retain human CAM, tooling and first-article approval; use conservative parameters, sister tools, tool-life counters and mandatory probing after high-risk cuts. Interlock unloading until the machining cycle and tool-integrity checks both pass. |
| Robot collision with CNC, fixture or workpiece | High | Safety-rated joint torque or force limits, independent safe-position or envelope monitoring, CNC door/chuck/spindle interlocks and guarded low-speed approach; validate stopping performance throughout the workspace. System-level integration and combined mobile-platform/manipulator hazards must be assessed, rather than treating the arm and base separately (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016). | Define station-specific safe corridors and forbidden zones; mechanically stabilize the base, verify registration before entering the machine and use reduced speed near hard structures. Apply safety-rated monitored stop or speed-and-separation monitoring where people can enter; perform recovery only under controlled manual mode. |
| Optics contamination or handling damage | High | Inspect capped components and mounting surfaces under controlled illumination; particle, fluorescence or dark-field inspection where justified; monitor gripper force and verify protective caps remain present until final installation. | Keep optics in sealed trays and assemble in a clean enclosure using non-shedding tooling, gloves and filtered air. Have a person perform final cleanliness acceptance, M85 lens threading, optical alignment and galvo calibration because scanner performance is sensitive to assembly-specific optical and mechanical errors. |
| Wrong part picked or assembled | High | Barcode, Data Matrix or RFID identity check at source and destination; vision confirmation of geometry and orientation; kit-tray weight/completeness check; recipe-to-part-number interlock and fastener-count reconciliation. Reliable object recognition and coordination remain manufacturing-robot deployment barriers (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000047). | Use one-part-per-pocket kits, uniquely keyed nests, segregated fastener feeders and electronic work instructions tied to the serial-number build record. Require two independent identifiers for look-alike or safety-critical parts and stop for human disposition on any mismatch. |


*Table: Key failure modes for the proposed mobile-manipulator machining and assembly cell, with practical detection and mitigation controls. Severity reflects potential damage to personnel, machines, high-value components, or latent product quality.*

Include rows for: mechanical hardware setup (MiR+UR mounting, cabling, docking stations), safety risk assessment and documentation, station registration and accuracy validation, gripper/end-effector design and fabrication, CNC machine-tending programs (mill and lathe), assembly programs (~90 steps), vision/sensor commissioning, process validation and debugging, safety validation and acceptance testing, training, total commissioning, actual build (machining), actual build (assembly), total to produce one machine. Add notes explaining this is an author's estimate informed by published data ranges."}

messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-02)

| Activity | Mobile-Manipulator Cell (person-hours estimate) | Manual Build (person-hours estimate) | Notes/Source |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Mechanical hardware setup: MiR–UR mounting, cabling, docking stations | 60–120 | 0–8 | **Author’s estimate.** Includes two mobile platforms, arm mounts, utilities, tool racks, charging, docking or stabilization, and CNC interfaces. Integrated mobile manipulators require system-level treatment rather than separate arm/base integration (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016). |
| Safety risk assessment and documentation | 80–160 | 8–24 | **Author’s estimate.** Mobile manipulation, CNC access, sharp tools, suspended loads, collaborative contact, and shop traffic require an iterative ISO 12100 and ISO 10218 assessment; manual work still needs ordinary shop controls (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011). |
| Station registration and accuracy validation | 40–80 | 0 | **Author’s estimate.** Covers AprilTag and hand–eye calibration, datum probing, error budgets, repeated docking trials, and acceptance limits. Examples range from 50–100 mm error with SLAM alone to 10 mm or less with fiducials, 0.19 mm vision-compensated offset, and ±0.12 mm after structured station calibration (pqac-00000034, pqac-00000035). |
| Gripper and end-effector design and fabrication | 200–400 | 24–60 | **Author’s estimate.** Robot scope includes part grippers, vacuum tooling, nutrunners, O-ring tools, compliant insertion tools, tool changing, sensing, and storage. Custom fixtures and grippers are major reintegration burdens (pqac-00000047, pqac-00000051). |
| CNC machine-tending programs: mill and lathe | 100–180 | 60–140 | **Author’s estimate.** Robot effort covers doors, chuck and vise interaction, chip cleaning, guarded approaches, seating checks, recovery logic, and machine I/O, in addition to human CAM and first-article work required in both cases. Published mobile machine tending remains predominantly prototype or conceptual (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000036, pqac-00000038). |
| Assembly programs: approximately 90 steps | 300–600 | 8–24 | **Author’s estimate.** Assumes an average of 3–7 engineering hours per robotic step after reuse of common skills; O-rings, angle-head fastening, bearings, optics, and deformable components need more. Minute-scale programming applies to simple cobot screwdriving, not complete integration and recovery behavior (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000042, pqac-00000043). |
| Vision and sensor commissioning | 100–220 | 0 | **Author’s estimate.** Includes hand–eye calibration, fiducial detection, lighting, part-pose estimation, force/torque thresholds, gripper checks, and gauge interfaces. Fragile perception and inadequate sensor characterization remain deployment barriers (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000047). |
| Process validation and debugging | 250–500 | 24–60 | **Author’s estimate.** Includes repeated trials, fault injection, recovery testing, torque–angle envelopes, seating signatures, O-ring inspection, dropped-part handling, and CNC exceptions. Screwdriving fault recognition around 90–97% still requires process-specific teaching and validation (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000039). |
| Safety validation and acceptance testing | 80–160 | 8–16 | **Author’s estimate.** Includes stopping tests, collaborative-contact tests where applicable, interlock verification, speed-and-separation tests, CNC interface faults, and documented acceptance. PFL validation requires force and pressure measurements rather than reliance on the cobot label (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000014, pqac-00000053, pqac-00000054). |
| Operator and maintenance training | 24–48 | 4–8 | **Author’s estimate.** Robot training covers mission control, tool changes, recovery, safe manual mode, rejected operations, and maintenance. External-integrator dependence can impede later modifications and repairs (pqac-00000044, pqac-00000049). |
| **Total commissioning before the first machine** | **1,230–2,470** | **140–340** | **Author’s estimate obtained by summing the rows above.** No published benchmark exists for this exact cell. Conventional screwdriving automation is reported at 8–17 weeks, while NIST identifies integration time, programming, sensing, safety, and support as persistent barriers (pqac-00000042, pqac-00000044, pqac-00000046, pqac-00000050). |
| Actual build: machining and associated tending | 120–220 | 100–180 | **Author’s estimate.** Both cases retain human CAM, tool setting, first articles, heavy-plate lifting, inspection, and exception handling. Robot tending reduces attendance during cutting but adds cleaning, registration, and recovery overhead for a single build. |
| Actual build: cleaning, kitting, and assembly | 80–160 | 120–220 | **Author’s estimate of direct person-hours.** Robots can reduce repetitive screwdriving, transfer, washing, and kitting labor, but people remain necessary for routing, optics, difficult seals, fittings, welding, measurement exceptions, and hoisted integration. General three-dimensional deformable-object routing remains unresolved (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000020). |
| **Total person-hours to produce one machine** | **1,430–2,850** | **360–740** | **Author’s estimate informed by published evidence, not a measured result.** For one machine, robotic commissioning dominates and is unlikely to be recovered unless the cell is itself a research deliverable or its programs and tooling will be reused. |


*Table: Estimated direct person-hours for commissioning and using the proposed mobile-manipulator cell compared with producing the machine manually. The ranges are author estimates informed by published deployment, calibration, safety, and programming evidence because no source reports this exact application.*

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):

        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1
        - PHASE2: Phase 2
        - PHASE3: Phase 3
        - PHASE4: Phase 4
        - NA: Not Applicable

    StandardAge:
        - CHILD: Child
        - ADULT: Adult
        - OLDER_ADULT: Older Adult

    Status:
        - RECRUITING: Currently recruiting participants
        - ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING: Active but not recruiting
        - COMPLETED: Study completed
        - ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION: Enrolling by invitation only
        - NOT_YET_RECRUITING: Not yet recruiting
        - SUSPENDED: Study suspended
        - TERMINATED: Study terminated
        - WITHDRAWN: Study withdrawn
        - AVAILABLE: Available

        - TEMPORARILY_NOT_AVAILABLE: Temporarily not available
        - APPROVED_FOR_MARKETING: Approved for marketing
        - WITHHELD: Withheld
        - UNKNOWN: Unknown status

    StudyType:
        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies
        - OBSERVATIONAL: Observational studies
        - EXPANDED_ACCESS: Expanded access studies

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment
        - PREVENTION: Prevention
        - DIAGNOSTIC: Diagnostic
        - ECT: Educational/Counseling/Training
        - SUPPORTIVE_CARE: Supportive Care

Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string encoding an object with an "objectives" list;
never pass objectives separately.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

you must use the gather_evidence tool.

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.title: Text Name

Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation

Use the tools to answer the question: We are checking, in simulation, whether two collaborative robot arms (Universal Robots UR12e, the renamed UR10e: 12.5 kg payload including tooling, 1300 mm reach, built-in force/torque sensing), each on a MiR250 mobile base (docking to markers within about +-3 mm, then re-registering each station from an AprilTag with a wrist camera), could make and assemble a one-off desktop laser powder bed fusion machine in a university shop: unpacking deliveries, sawing bar, loading and unloading a Haas VF-4 vertical mill (with an HRT210 4th axis) and a Haas ST-10-class CNC lathe, deburring, ultrasonic washing, measuring, kitting parts onto a long table, then assembling about 90 steps: FKM O-rings in face glands, half-dovetail grooves and internal rod-gland grooves (with ring loaders, rollers and mandrels as end-of-arm tools), about 130 M3-M6 stainless screws driven with a nutrunner and an angle-head nutrunner, dowel pins, helical inserts, bearings, a ball screw and linear rail, cartridge heaters and thermocouples, optics (a galvo scan head, an f-theta lens on an M85 thread), and a final integration where a person with a hoist moves the 84 kg process module onto a storage-system tray. Our current plan keeps a person for: loading a 34.7 kg aluminium plate blank onto the mill with a vacuum tube lifter, CAM and first-article runs, tool setting, TIG welding a thin-wall 316L tube to flanges, reading bore and height gauges, routing hoses, fibres and cables, threading small fittings with tubes attached, installing a felt-and-PTFE bore seal, and lifting anything over the arms' combined payload.

Please review this plan critically, with sources: (1) published examples and industrial practice of mobile manipulators (AMR plus cobot) tending CNC machines and doing assembly in high-mix, low-volume or one-off settings: achieved positioning accuracy after docking and re-registration, uptime and failure rates, cycle-time penalties, commissioning effort per new task, and what still needed people; (2) which of the steps above are realistic for cobots today and which are not, and whether our person-only list is too long or too short (for example: can cobots route cables and hoses, install felt seals, TIG weld one-off parts, read bore gauges, thread fittings with tubing attached, handle 15-35 kg plates as a pair); (3) the hardest failure modes to expect (chips and coolant, fixture seating, part pose errors, cross-threading and galling of stainless screws, dropping parts, O-ring twist), and how they are detected; (4) safety for a shop where people and mobile manipulators work together: ISO 10218-1/-2 (2025), ISO/TS 15066, ANSI/A3 R15.08 for industrial mobile robots, and what a risk assessment for this cell would need; (5) a realistic estimate of the person-hours and calendar time to commission such a cell for one machine compared with simply building it by hand. Give concrete numbers where they exist and say clearly where you are estimating.

Start by making a plan, and update the plan as you go. Your answer will be returned to the user when all plan objectives are completed. Be thorough and ensure your evidence matches the user's question.

Abstract:
The rapid evolution of automation has become a defining phenomenon of the modern era, underscoring its great influence on industries and economies. Since the First Industrial Revolution, advancements in technology have consistently transformed manufacturing processes, progressively introducing mechanization, electrification, and digitalization. The current Fifth Industrial Revolution incorporates these changes through the integration of robotics, cobots (collaborative robots), and AI-driven (Artificial Intelligence) systems, representing unprecedented levels of human–machine collaboration. This paper examines the historical evolution of automation and industrial robotics and, based on the current state of the art, highlights the current standing of its economic and societal impacts. The adoption of automation and robotization in the supply chain and manufacturing has significantly enhanced productivity and precision, reducing errors and operational costs. However, it has also contributed to job displacement, especially in repetitive and manual tasks, necessitating the reskilling of the human workforce. Automation brings two main financial effects: it reduces long-term labor costs and boosts efficiency, but the upfront investments in advanced robotics and infrastructure are significant. Understanding these dynamics is crucial for navigating the challenges and opportunities presented by automation, which ensures a balanced approach to economic growth, workforce development, and technological adoption across all sectors influenced by successive industrial revolutions.

Abstract:
The high-mix, low-volume (HMLV) industry has seen growth in the need for product customisation with research to increase manufacturers’ flexibility for the variation in market demands. This paper reviews 152 documents from 2000 to October 2022, discussing work related to HMLV production. From an industrial perspective, this paper analyses the industries with HMLV, revealing production sectors and research areas, categorising the developed work, type of validation, and applications. The results show that most work is not industry-specific, with production planning as the central aspect of the research. While other parts of the production processes and value chain received less attention, the semiconductor and electronics industries are the two most researched with substantial validation, leaving gaps in other industries. Earlier work primarily focused on the theoretical development of production planning; however, the development of Industry 4.0 technologies advocates decision support systems for reactive production planning. This period sees the rise in robotics and automation, with improved robotics capability and human—robot collaboration. Assembly assistance systems were developed for manual production to aid operators in managing the variety of information. This paper serves as a reference for the HMLV manufacturing industry in a structured manner while identifying potential for future research in this field.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Manual alignment between the trocar, surgical instrument, and robot during minimally invasive surgery (MIS) can be time-consuming and error-prone, and many existing systems do not provide autonomous localization and pose estimation. This paper presents an artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted, vision-guided framework for automated localization and positioning of the ATHENA parallel surgical robot. The proposed approach combines an Intel RealSense RGB–depth (RGB-D) camera with a You Only Look Once version 11 (YOLO11) object detection model to estimate the 3D spatial coordinates of key surgical components in real time. The estimated coordinates are streamed over Transmission Control Protocol/Internet Protocol (TCP/IP) to a programmable logic controller (PLC) using Modbus/TCP, enabling closed-loop robot positioning for automated docking. Experimental validation in a controlled setup designed to replicate key intraoperative constraints demonstrated submillimeter positioning accuracy (≤0.8 mm), an average end-to-end latency of 67 ms, and a 42% reduction in setup time compared with manual alignment, while remaining robust under variable lighting. These results indicate that the proposed perception-to-control pipeline is a practical step toward reliable autonomous robotic docking in MIS workflows.</jats:p>

Abstract:
This contribution summarizes the current state of research regarding so‐called sensor‐integrating machine elements as an enabler of digitalization in mechanical engineering and——if available—their application in industry. The focus is on the methodical aspects of the development of these machine elements in general as well as specific sensor‐integrating machine elements that are either already in use or currently under development. Developmental aspects include the robust design of initially evaluated concepts for sensor‐integrating machine elements as well as their modularization. Smart materials with sensory functions are included in the analysis as well as the differentiation with regard to add‐on sensors. The aim of the authors interlinked by a special research program funded by the German Research Foundation (DFG) is to facilitate the exchange with other researchers with the help of the comprehensive overview given in this contribution. The contribution concludes with a brief discussion of open challenges, such as the energy supply and data transfer in rotating systems and also data security.

Abstract:
Soft robotic actuators can simplify the design of controllers when operating in contact-rich environments. Importantly, their passive compliance fundamentally alters contact mechanics by smoothing impacts and distributing forces over large areas. By integrating soft actuators, we can perform high-impact, dynamic, and contact-rich tasks that are challenging or impossible for traditional rigid robots. In order to explore the benefits of passive structural compliance and learn to utilize it effectively, we present a prototype robotic torso named Baloo. Baloo's hybrid soft-rigid design incorporates both adaptability from soft components and strength from rigid components with two meter-long, pneumatic robot arms mounted on a rigid torso. The hybrid design is capable of lifting end effector payloads of up to 19 kg, far exceeding many hybrid robot designs. Such payloads are competitive with similar-sized rigid robots, but with a much higher strength-to-weight ratio. Through 30 physical whole-body grasping experiments, we also demonstrate how a simple control strategy can generalize for effective lifting across six challenging objects with diverse shapes, sizes, and weights. A 100% success rate across all objects--achieved with the simple control strategy--underscores the potential of our hybrid soft-rigid robot design for contact-rich, whole-body tasks.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Soft robotics research has rapidly incorporated Additive Manufacturing (AM) into its standard prototyping repertoire. While numerous publications have highlighted the suitability of AM for producing soft pneumatic actuators, fluidic components, and lightweight structures, their integration into an industry-like robotic arm has not yet been shown. Against this background, a pneumatically actuated robot was developed that incorporates additively manufactured soft structures into rigid articulated hinges that generally allow for integration into today’s industrial production lines. The development of the robot, including pneumatic soft rotary bellows and rotary vane actuators (RVAs), is summarized, and its functionality is proven. It was found that using AM can increase the structural stiffness of robot links to a significant degree as manufacturing-related constraints in topology optimization are largely eliminated. Moreover, it was found that multi-material polyjet printing of soft rotary bellows actuators allows for highly integrated designs that provide low leakage and friction. However, these soft rotary actuators are still inferior in terms of endurance and performance if compared to AM replicas of RVAs. Our work narrows the gap between soft robotics research and today’s industrial applications, may realign research directions, and may provide impulses for the industry towards soft robotics and AM.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Human–robot collaboration is currently one of the frontiers of industrial robot implementation. In parallel, the use of robots and robotic devices is increasing in several fields, substituting humans in “4D”—dull, dirty, dangerous, and delicate—tasks, and such a trend is boosted by the recent need for social distancing. New challenges in safety assessment and verification arise, due to both the closer and closer human–robot interaction, common for the different application domains, and the broadening of user audience, which is now very diverse. The present paper discusses a cross-domain approach towards the definition of step-by-step validation procedures for collaborative robotic applications. To outline the context, the standardization framework is analyzed, especially from the perspective of safety testing and assessment. Afterwards, some testing procedures based on safety skills, developed within the framework of the European project COVR, are discussed and exemplary presented.

Abstract:
An in‐depth understanding of the risks related to robotic systems is crucial to guarantee safety throughout all stages of robot design and operations. This required a thorough risk assessment following international standards. This study presents a systematic review of previous research on safety considerations in the design of robotic systems, concentrating exclusively on peer‐reviewed articles. A search method was developed to collect relevant articles, using keywords such as safety, fault, risk evaluation, safety evaluation, risk assessment, and ergonomics, among others. The keyword “robot” was utilized to bias the search results, which helped to narrow down collected articles to papers directly related to robotics. The risk assessment process includes recognizing machine shortcomings, recognizing threats, evaluating risk, and articulating a standardized computerized risk strategy. Mathematical analysis plays a crucial role in assessing the technical and social behavior of robots in different applications. Generally, injury associated with robots arises from errors during risk assessment. The Risk Ranking Number (HRN) is employed to quantify the degree of safety, incorporating factors like the possibility of occurrence and magnitude of potential hazard. In robot design, the main attention should be on minimizing/eradicating physical hazards and optimizing control mechanisms. Algorithms like force limitation and obstacle avoidance can minimize injury risk, especially during robot–human interactions. The review underscores the critical importance of establishing comprehensive risk assessment frameworks and utilizing safety models, algorithms, and functions as crucial tools to safeguard the integrity and security of robotic systems.

Abstract:
<jats:p>This study presents an integrated experimental and modeling framework to
investigate human–robot collision dynamics involving a collaborative manipulator (KUKA
LBR iiwa 14 R820). A dedicated impact test prototype was developed to reproduce con-
trolled contact scenarios between the robot and human body analogues under various
dynamic conditions. The experimental setup enables the acquisition of synchronized force,
velocities, and displacement signals during contact events. This data are used to calibrate
and validate a set of contact models, ranging from classical formulations such as Hertz
and Hunt–Crossley to more recent supervised machine learning models. The proposed
methodology allows a quantitative assessment of model accuracy and physical consistency 
in replicating real collision phenomena. Furthermore, the effective mass of the robot along 
its kinematic chain is estimated to compute impact energy and predict the interaction
severity according to ISO 10218-1/2:2025 safety limits. The results highlight the trade-off
between model complexity and predictive capability, offering alternative guidelines for
collision severity evaluation in collaborative robotics applications.</jats:p>

Abstract:
The use of collaborative robots in the industrial domain has significantly grown in the last years, allowing humans to operate in the same workspace occupied by robots without any physical barriers. Understandably, the safety of the human operator has been a major concern both for researchers and regulatory bodies. The power and force limited modality of robots is of particular interest in that sense, being used in order to bound the energy of eventual collisions when a close physical interaction with humans is necessary. Such an interaction modality allows the robotic system to operate without the use of barriers, but a measurement of the force and pressure occurring due to a contact must be provided as part of the risk assessment. However, the precise procedure to follow in order to reliably provide such measures is still unclear for users and system integrators willing to self-assess the safety of their own collaborative robotic system. In this work, the repeatability and reliability of such testing procedures and measures are analyzed with an interlaboratory comparison approach, with the aim to establish the degree of variability possibly encountered when performing the same test under slightly different conditions.

This challenge included assembly of standard, commercially available industrial parts into 2D and 3D assemblies. Abstract:
This paper proposes a set of tactile based skills to perform robotic cable routing operations for deformable linear objects (DLOs) characterized by considerable stiffness and constrained at both ends. In particular, tactile data are exploited to reconstruct the shape of the grasped portion of the DLO and to estimate the future local one. This information is exploited to obtain a grasping configuration aligned to the local shape of the DLO, starting from a rough initial grasping pose, and to follow the DLO's contour in the three-dimensional space. Taking into account the distance travelled along the arc length of the DLO, the robot can detect the cable segments that must be firmly grasped and inserted in intermediate clips, continuing then to slide along the contour until the next DLO's portion, that has to be clipped, is reached. The proposed skills are experimentally validated with an industrial robot on different DLOs in several configurations and on a cable routing use case.

Abstract:
Currently, cables are manually installed in aircraft manufacturing scenarios. The utilization of robots in cable assemblies can enhance efficiency and ensure quality, presenting great promise for the future. However, the assembly process must control the shape of the cables, which is a significant challenge for robots. On the one hand, cables have high degrees of freedom in space, making accurate modeling of cable dynamics for robotic arm manipulation difficult; on the other hand, cable deformation has uncertainty, and the applied forces cause simultaneous deformation and motion, which is difficult to control. To address these problems, this study proposes a cable‐shape control method based on graph neural networks and online visual shape‐servoing. The method first approximates cable dynamics with a graph neural network. Then, in practice, the learnt model is used alongside visual‐based shape‐servoing to generate optimal robotic arm movements, controlling the cable to attain the desired shape. In the experiments, precise control of three different cable types is realized, and an example of a completed cable assembly is shown.

However, DLOs pose several challenges for robot-based automation due to the inherent complexity of deformation and, consequentially, the difficulties in anticipating the behavior of DLOs in dynamic situations. Although existing studies have addressed isolated subproblems like shape tracking, grasping, and shape control, there has been limited exploration of integrated workflows that combine these individual processes. To address this gap, we propose an object-centric perception and planning framework to achieve a comprehensive DLO assembly process throughout the industrial value chain. The framework utilizes visual and tactile information to track the DLO's shape as well as contact state across different stages, which facilitates effective planning of robot actions. Our approach encompasses robot-based bin picking of DLOs from cluttered environments, followed by a coordinated handover to two additional robots that mount the DLOs onto designated fixtures. Real-world experiments employing a setup with multiple robots demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach and its relevance to industrial scenarios.

Abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Deformable linear objects (DLOs) are widely encountered in everyday life, taking forms such as plastic tubes, wires, ropes, and cables. They are prevalent across diverse settings, including industrial, domestic, and medical environments, as well as in outdoor applications like electric power lines, subaquatic cables, and aerial transport systems. These objects are termed
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">deformable</jats:italic>
                    due to their ability to undergo significant shape changes under external forces, and
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">linear</jats:italic>
                    because their length vastly exceeds their cross-sectional dimensions. Despite their importance and widespread presence, developing robotic systems capable of interacting with DLOs poses numerous challenges. This survey presents a comprehensive review of the state-of-the-art methods developed over the past decade to address these challenges. It covers key areas including physical and data-driven modeling techniques, simulation environments, perception approaches based on vision and tactile sensing, as well as strategies for estimation, planning, and control. It also reviews common manipulation tasks such as grasping, shaping, routing, knotting, suturing, and transport. The survey concludes with a critical discussion of current limitations and outlines promising directions for future research.
                  </jats:p>

Abstract:
Manipulating a deformable linear object (DLO) such as wire, cable, and rope is a common yet challenging task due to their high degrees of freedom and complex deformation behaviors, especially in an environment with obstacles. Existing local control methods are efficient but prone to failure in complex scenarios, while precise global planners are computationally intensive and difficult to deploy. This paper presents an efficient, easy-to-deploy framework for collision-free DLO manipulation using mobile manipulators. We demonstrate the effectiveness of leveraging standard planning tools for high-dimensional DLO manipulation without requiring custom planners or extensive data-driven models. Our approach combines an off-the-shelf global planner with a real-time local controller. The global planner approximates the DLO as a series of rigid links connected by spherical joints, enabling rapid path planning without the need for problem-specific planners or large datasets. The local controller employs control barrier functions (CBFs) to enforce safety constraints, maintain the DLO integrity, prevent overstress, and handle obstacle avoidance. It compensates for modeling inaccuracies by using a state-of-the-art position-based dynamics technique that approximates physical properties like Young's and shear moduli. We validate our framework through extensive simulations and real-world demonstrations. In complex obstacle scenarios-including tent pole transport, corridor navigation, and tasks requiring varied stiffness-our method achieves a 100% success rate over thousands of trials, with significantly reduced planning times compared to state-of-the-art techniques. Real-world experiments include transportation of a tent pole and a rope using mobile manipulators. We share our ROS-based implementation to facilitate adoption in various applications.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Manipulation robotique d'objets linéaires déformables basée sur la vision</jats:title>
                <jats:p xml:lang="fr">En robotique, la manipulation d'objets déformables reçoit moins d'attention que celle d'objets rigides. Pourtant, de nombreux objets dans la vie réelle sont déformables. La recherche sur la manipulation d'objets déformables est indispensable pour doter les robots d'une dextérité de manipulation totale. La difficulté majeure de ce problème est que déformation de l'objet a un espace de configurations de dimensions infinie, tandis que les entrées du robots sont limitées. Dans le cadre de VERSATILE, un projet H2020 axé sur l'automatisation industrielle à l'aide de robots, nous avons axé nos recherches sur la manipulation d'objets déformables linéaires (câbles) par retour visuel.Une caractéristique de la manipulation des objets déformables est que la forme de l'objet change pendant la manipulation. Par conséquent, un problème important consiste à contrôler la forme de l'objet pendant la manipulation. Nous avons abordé le problème du contrôle de forme en exploitant le retour visuel.Dans un premier temps, nous avons représenté la forme de l'objet avec une série de Fourier. Nous estimons et mettons à jour la matrice d'interaction en ligne, puis nous concevons le contrôleur pour contrôler la forme.Ensuite, au lieu d'utiliser une caractéristique définie par l'humain pour le paramétrage, nous avons laissé le robot apprendre automatiquement les vecteurs de caractéristiques à partir des données visuelles. Nous proposons une méthode qui permet au robot de générer simultanément - et à partir des mêmes données - un vecteur de caractéristiques ainsi que la matrice d'interaction. Cette méthode nécessite un minimum de données pour l'initialisation. L'apprentissage et le contrôle peuvent être effectués en ligne de manière adaptative. Nous pouvons appliquer la même méthode à la manipulation d'objets rigides, directement et sans modification.Ces deux travaux ne requièrent aucune calibration de la caméra et ont été validés avec des expérimentations de robotique réelle.Un autre domaine d'importance dans la manipulation d'objets déformables est l'utilisation de contacts externes pour contrôler la forme de l'objet. Les contacts externes peuvent et doivent être utilisés pour la manipulation d'objets déformables. Nous considérons un scénario fréquent dans l'industrie - l'acheminement de câbles avec des contacts externes comme processus à automatiser avec notre robot. Nous proposons un algorithme de planification qui permet au robot d'utiliser des contacts pour déformer le câble et pour obtenir la configuration souhaitée. Des expériences robotiques réelles avec différents scénarios de placement de contacts permettent de valider nos algorithmes.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Starting in the 1970s with robots that were physically isolated from contact with their human co-workers, robots now collaborate with human workers towards a common task goal in a shared workspace. This type of robotic device represents a new era of workplace automation. Industrial robotics is rapidly evolving due to advances in sensor technology, artificial intelligence (AI), wireless communications, mechanical engineering, and materials science. While these new robotic devices are used mainly in manufacturing and warehousing, human-robot collaboration is now seen across multiple goods-producing and service-delivery industry sectors. Assessing and controlling the risks of human-robot collaboration is a critical challenge for occupational safety and health research and practice as industrial robotics becomes a pervasive feature of the future of work. Understanding the physical, psychosocial, work organization, and cybersecurity risks associated with the increasing use of robotic technologies is critical to ensuring the safe development and implementation of industrial robotics. This commentary provides a brief review of the uses of robotic technologies across selected industry sectors; the risks of current and future industrial robotic applications for worker and employer alike; strategies for integrating human-robot collaboration into a health and safety management system; and the role of robotic safety standards in the future of work.

Abstract:
Enabling technologies that drive Industry 4.0 and smart factories are pushing in new equipment and system development also to prevent human workers from repetitive and non-ergonomic tasks inside manufacturing plants. One of these tasks is the order-picking which consists in collecting parts from the warehouse and distributing them among the workstations and vice-versa. That task can be completely performed by a Mobile Manipulator that is composed by an industrial manipulator assembled on a Mobile Robot. Although the Mobile Manipulators implementation brings advantages to industrial applications, they are still not widely used due to the lack of dedicated standards on control and safety. Furthermore, there are few integrated solutions and no specific or reference point allowing the safe integration of mobile robots and cobots (already owned by company). This work faces the integration of a generic mobile robot and collaborative robot selected from an identified set of both systems. The paper presents a safe and flexible mechatronic interface developed by using MBSE principles, multi-domain modeling, and adopting preliminary assumptions on the hardware and software synchronization level of both involved systems. The interface enables the re-using of owned robot systems differently from their native tasks. Furthermore, it provides an additional and redundant safety level by enabling power and force limiting both during cobot positioning and control system faulting.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Industrial mobile robots are increasingly deployed in warehouses and production sites and interaction takes place with different stakeholders from different disciplines. In such sociotechnical settings, terminology shapes mental models and perceptions that influence trust, interaction, and safe collaboration. Key labels such as driverless transport vehicle (DTV), automated guided vehicle (AGV), autonomous mobile robot (AMR) and mobile robot (MR) are used inconsistently across standards, industry practice and academic literature. It remains unclear how experts actually interpret these terms in professional communication, since the terms are only in part defined by standards and perceived differently throughout the industry. We address this gap with an online survey of 53 mobile robotics experts. Spontaneous associations, the perceived distinctiveness between pairs of terms, consistency with general terminology statements and attributed technical characteristics are identified. The results are contrasted with normative references and interoperability initiatives. The findings indicate systematic, term-specific perceptions. Participants report divergent perceptions, conflicting definitions and a lack of uniform terminology. Experts rated AGV and DTV as largely indistinguishable (relative effect = −0.51/-1), but considered AGV and AMR clearly more separable (0.37/1), while MR functioned as a broad umbrella term that evoked capability-related associations yet remained ambiguous. Based on these ambiguities, we synthesize recommendations for how terminology should be communicated and qualified in industrial mobile robotics to reduce expectation gaps across stakeholder groups and facilitate a joint, uniform understanding.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Occupational Applications Autonomous mobile robots are used in manufacturing and warehousing industries, to transport material across the facility and deliver parts to work cells. Human workers might encounter or interact with these robots in aisle ways or at their workstation. It is important to consider factors that impact worker safety and trust when implementing autonomous mobile robots in the workplace. This paper reviews prior research that aims to improve the safety of human-robot interaction with autonomous mobile robots and identifies needs for future research. Researchers used a variety of questionnaires and behavioral assessment methods to measure perceived safety. Factors such as robot appearance, approach speed, and approach direction, significantly affect perceived safety. Additionally, projection of signals on the floor, turn signals, and haptic communication devices, can improve the predictability and overall safety of robot navigation. Technical Abstract Introduction: Autonomous mobile robots are rapidly emerging in the workplace, which potentially creates new hazards for human workers that interact with them. Purpose: We aimed to systematically review previous research on human-robot interaction with autonomous mobile robots that apply to industrial environments, and to identify research needs to improve worker safety and trust. Methods: We completed a systematic review following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses methodology. We focused on articles that contained experiments with human participants and that included findings associated with improving safety and/or trust of workers who interact with mobile robots in industrial environments. We identified 50 articles that fit inclusion/exclusion criteria for the review. Results: Almost all of the reported experiments were conducted in a controlled laboratory setting. There were 27 different types of autonomous mobile robots. Only two studies involved industrial mobile robots that were commercially available and could be implemented in an industrial environment. Most studies used questionnaires, with the most common topic relating to participant perceptions of various robot traits, while few directly evaluated perceived safety and trust using questionnaires. Behavioral and physiological assessment methods were used in 70% and 8% of the studies, respectively. Separation distance between the participant and robot was the most common behavioral assessment method. A variety of robot characteristics were found to have a significant effect on human perception of safety and other similar concepts. Conclusions: Future research requires rigorous reporting of participant demographics and experience level with robots. We found that 34% and 44% of references failed to report the mean age of their participant sample and their experience with robots, respectively. Among several gaps that we identified in the literature were a lack of field experiments, sparse research involving multiple mobile robots, and limited use of industrial mobile robots in experiments with human participants.

Through an exploration of practical use cases, it elucidates how ROS facilitates the development and implementation of AMRs, reshaping various industrial processes. The article concludes that the combined use of Digital Twin technologies, collaborative robots and MCDM-based decision support represents a promising direction for implementing automation in small-batch production.</jats:p>
