<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    This paper presents an online scheduling framework for a multi-compartment Automated Guided Vehicle (AGV) with optional onboard cobot, embedded in a Digital Twin environment that provides real-time machine-state data. The scheduler is a Genetic Algorithm (GA) with mission-index encoding and feasibility-by-construction initialization, generating valid sequences under capacity, traceability, and precedence constraints. To isolate the value of machine-state awareness, the GA operates in two modes: an RPT-blind baseline using logistics data only, and an RPT-aware extension that integrates machine Remaining Processing Time (RPT) into feasibility and fitness evaluation. Validation across eleven scenarios on a precision aerospace workshop reveals that the impact of RPT-awareness is regime-dependent. In non-saturated and capacity-constrained settings, readiness-driven synchronization reduces transport waste (Trip Time −34–51%, Empty Trip Time −54–70% vs. RPT-blind) but increases makespan by 5–11%, because conservative waiting can delay feeding of bottleneck resources. In coordination-sensitive and high-mix regimes, RPT-awareness improves both dimensions simultaneously, reducing makespan by up to 10% (810
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:tex-math>$$\rightarrow$$</jats:tex-math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    728 min) alongside comparable logistics gains. Relative to the FIFO baseline representing current industrial practice, GA-based automation reduces Trip Time by 15–60% and Empty Trip Time by 15–77%. RPT-awareness also enables proactive cobot scheduling, completing all eligible inline missions (up to 29 per shift versus 4–9 in RPT-blind mode). The results indicate that RPT-aware scheduling is most effective where coordination complexity, rather than processing capacity, bounds system performance.

The excerpt characterizes robotic cable and hose routing as an emerging but incomplete capability. Existing systems address following deformable linear objects (DLOs), managing contacts with clips and pegs, routing through slots, and threading. Local execution generally depends on tactile or force sensing, while vision is used primarily for global planning. Robots can perform selected autonomous subtasks: learned visual policies have been demonstrated for slot insertion, tactile feedback can guide weaving through slots, and force-based control can regulate clipping and detect contact states. However, much of the state of the art still relies on scripted or heuristic motion primitives—such as sliding, grasping, reorienting, clipping, and weaving—that must be coordinated by a higher-level planner. Reinforcement learning and multimodal sensing show promise for more adaptive behavior, and model-predictive control with learned wire dynamics has also been explored. Key limitations include the dominance of 2D planar experiments, limited coverage of full 3D routing and dynamic harnessing, and continued reliance on specialized external sensing and preprogrammed behaviors. The cited literature covers plastic and elastic DLOs, but only a subset addresses threading or slot insertion, and the need to robustly coordinate perception, contact management, planning, and execution remains unresolved.

Threading is a higher-precision subtask involving insertion through designated openings, such as needle-like holes or industrial assemblies. Existing systems commonly use action-based planning with scripted or learned reusable motion primitives, including clipping and insertion, rather than fully general autonomous manipulation. The literature is organized around DLO following, contact management, routing-sequence parsing and planning, and threading. Tactile and force sensing are especially important for local execution: they provide feedback for grip adjustment, tension maintenance, sliding, and alignment. Vision is primarily used for global route planning. The NIST Assembly Task Board is emerging as a standardized benchmark for routing and supports reproducible comparisons, although it represents a simplified scenario. The main limitations are the field’s strong bias toward 2D planar setups, simplified environments, and established task configurations. Full 3D routing, dynamic harnessing, complex contact-rich interactions, and realistic elastoplastic cables remain insufficiently studied. The excerpt indicates that autonomous routing is feasible for constrained clipping, following, and insertion scenarios, but robust general-purpose routing through arbitrary clips and channels remains an open research problem.

The excerpt identifies misalignment during the preliminary spiral insertion as the principal failure mode for robotic nut/screw-like insertion. Friction caused by the stud’s raised lip and by the threads can make the nut stick, prevent recovery from misalignment, or cause the part to hang insecurely and fall when released. A final downward push can help align a mostly aligned nut, and the authors report no observed cross-threading in their trials; therefore, the excerpt does not provide a demonstrated torque-angle method for detecting cross-threading. During successful threading, forces have a saw-tooth profile, while the final downward motion produces a descending staircase in Z-force. Torque-based stopping can also generate false positives: gripper contact with the base plate may create enough frictional torque to satisfy the stopping criterion even though the intended threading condition is not necessarily complete. The authors propose detecting failures from distinctive force/torque profiles and time distributions, potentially aborting actions early and triggering recovery actions such as regrasping or restarting localization. They emphasize that estimating the held part’s pose and relating force-torque data to part geometry is a missing capability. The excerpt contains no discussion of stainless-steel galling, stripped threads, or explicit detection of incorrect seating beyond force/torque patterns and stopping criteria.

Abstract:
It is well accepted that remanufacturing, the returning of a product that has reached the end of its service life to its original condition, is economically and environmentally beneficial. Robotizing disassembly can make remanufacturing even more cost-effective by removing a substantial proportion of the labour costs associated with dismantling end-of-life products for subsequent processing. As unplugging of press-fitted components is a common operation in disassembly, it is appropriate to investigate how it can be robotized. This paper discusses an unplugging technique, twist-and-pull or twisting-pulling, to reduce the axial frictional resistance during the unplugging process and enable a robot to perform it easily. Through theoretical modelling, simulations, and experimental analysis, the paper explores the interaction between twisting, pulling and axial friction reduction during unplugging. Analysis of the experimental, simulation and theoretical results has confirmed that for a small radial interference, twist-and-pull reduces the axial friction and the maximum required unplugging force.

Abstract:
In the human hand, high-density contact information provided by afferent neurons is essential for many human grasping and manipulation capabilities. In contrast, robotic tactile sensors, including the state-of-the-art SynTouch BioTac, are typically used to provide low-density contact information, such as contact location, center of pressure, and net force. Although useful, these data do not convey or leverage the rich information content that some tactile sensors naturally measure. This research extends robotic tactile sensing beyond reduced-order models through (1) the automated creation of a precise experimental tactile dataset for the BioTac over a diverse range of physical interactions, (2) a 3D finite-element (FE) model of the BioTac, which complements the experimental dataset with high-density, distributed contact data, (3) neural-network-based mappings from raw BioTac signals to not only low-dimensional experimental data, but also high-density FE deformation fields, and (4) mappings from the FE deformation fields to the raw signals themselves. The high-density data streams can provide a far greater quantity of interpretable information for grasping and manipulation algorithms than previously accessible. Datasets, CAD files for the experimental testbed, FE model files, and videos are available at https://sites.google.com/nvidia.com/tactiledata.

Abstract:
Automating aircraft manufacturing still relies heavily on human labor due to the complexity of the assembly processes and customization requirements. One key challenge is achieving precise positioning, especially for large aircraft structures, where errors can lead to substantial maintenance costs or part rejection. Existing solutions often require costly hardware or lack flexibility. Used in aircraft by the thousands, threaded fasteners, e.g., screws, bolts, and collars, are traditionally executed by fixed-base robots and usually have problems in being deployed in the mentioned manufacturing sites. This paper emphasizes the importance of error detection and classification for efficient and safe assembly of threaded fasteners, especially aeronautical collars. Safe assembly of threaded fasteners is paramount since acquiring sufficient data for training deep learning models poses challenges due to the rarity of failure cases and imbalanced datasets. The paper addresses this by proposing techniques like class weighting and data augmentation, specifically tailored for temporal series data, to improve classification performance. Furthermore, the paper introduces a novel problem-modeling approach, emphasizing metrics relevant to collar assembly rather than solely focusing on accuracy. This tailored approach enhances the models' capability to handle the challenges of threaded fastener assembly effectively.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Flexible automated assembly lines (FAALs) in Industry 4.0 require robust quality management that integrates operational data with systematic risk analysis. However, Process Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (PFMEA) documents are often developed during the design phase and not systematically updated with actual production data, leading to a gap between formal risk assessment and operational reality. This study addresses this gap by developing and validating an integrated data-driven framework that combines classical quality tools (process flow charts, check sheets, cause-and-effect diagrams, and Pareto analysis) with data-driven PFMEA, creating traceable links from operational logs to risk ratings. While individual quality tools are well-established, the core contribution of this work is a structured data transformation pipeline that creates traceable, auditable linkages from raw operational event logs to calibrated PFMEA ratings with quantified uncertainty—a combination not previously demonstrated for flexible assembly systems. The framework was applied to FMS-200, a modular FAAL for bearing units, consisting of eight stations and a common transfer system. Analysis of 186 failure events across 2743 assembly cycles, including 18 product configurations, identified 40 distinct failure modes with risk priority number (RPN) values ranging from 60 to 378, revealing that approximately 90% of the aggregated risk is associated with pneumatic systems. Monte Carlo uncertainty analysis (10,000 iterations) demonstrated robust rank stability, with the top five failure modes maintaining their relative ordering in over 90% of simulations. The framework provides production and quality managers with a systematic methodology to maintain PFMEA relevance through continuous data integration, enabling evidence-based prioritization of improvement actions.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Robotic assembly is one of the oldest and most challenging applications of robotics. In other areas of robotics, such as perception and grasping, simulation has rapidly accelerated research progress, particularly when combined with modern deep learning. However, accurately, efficiently, and robustly simulating the range of contact-rich interactions in assembly remains a longstanding challenge. In this work, we present Factory, a set of physics simulation methods and robot learning tools for such applications. We achieve real-time or faster simulation of a wide range of contact-rich scenes, including simultaneous simulation of 1000 nut-and-bolt interactions. We provide $60$ carefully-designed part models, 3 robotic assembly environments, and 7 robot controllers for training and testing virtual robots. Finally, we train and evaluate proof-of-concept reinforcement learning policies for nut-and-bolt assembly. We aim for Factory to open the doors to using simulation for robotic assembly, as well as many other contact-rich applications in robotics. Abstract:
<jats:p>A novel closed loop visual positioning system, termed YOLO–LaserGalvo (YLGS), is proposed for precise localization of welding torch tips in industrial welding automation. The proposed system integrates a monocular camera, an infrared laser distance sensor with a galvanometer scanner, and a customized deep learning detector based on an improved YOLOv11 model. In operation, the vision subsystem first detects the approximate image location of the torch tip using the YOLOv11-based model. Guided by this detection, the galvanometer steers the IR laser beam to that point and measures the distance to the torch tip. The distance feedback is then fused with the vision coordinates to compute the precise 3D position of the torch tip in real-time. Under complex illumination, the proposed YLGS system exhibits superior robustness compared with color-marker and ArUco baselines. Experimental evaluation shows that the system outperforms traditional color-marker and ArUco-based methods in terms of accuracy, robustness, and processing speed. This marker-free method provides high-precision torch positioning without requiring structured lighting or artificial markers. Its pedagogical implications in engineering education are also discussed. Potential future work includes extending the method to full 6-DOF pose estimation and integrating additional sensors for enhanced performance.</jats:p>

Abstract:
The three-dimensional (3D) size and morphology of high-temperature metal components need to be measured in real time during manufacturing processes, such as forging and rolling. Since the surface temperature of a metal component is very high during the forming and manufacturing process, manually measuring the size of a metal component at a close distance is difficult; hence, a non-contact measurement technology is required to complete the measurement. Recently, machine vision technology has been developed, which is a non-contact measurement technology that only needs to capture multiple images of a measured object to obtain the 3D size and morphology information, and this technology can be used in some extreme conditions. Machine vision technology has been widely used in industrial, agricultural, military and other fields, especially fields involving various high-temperature metal components. This paper provides a comprehensive review of the application of machine vision technology in measuring the 3D size and morphology of high-temperature metal components. Furthermore, according to the principle and method of measuring equipment structures, this review highlights two aspects in detail: laser scanning measurement and multi-view stereo vision technology. Special attention is paid to each method through comparisons and analyses to provide essential technical references for subsequent researchers.

Abstract:
Micro-opto-electro-mechanical systems (MOEMS) based mirrors with a suitable actuation range are often used for optical beam scanning applications. While several MOEMS scanners have been reported, they often have limitations with respect to their range of motion, field of view, mass, size and fabrication cost. In this work, we present a rotary micro-polygon scanner based on an electrostatic variable capacitance micromotor for laser beam steering applications. The miniaturized scanner consists of a hollow micro-polyhedron mirror with a base radius of <inline-formula> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$200 {\mu }\text{m}$ </tex-math></inline-formula> and a height of <inline-formula> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$400 {\mu }\text{m}$ </tex-math></inline-formula>. It is mounted on the rotor of a variable capacitance micromotor using an epoxy-based adhesive. The rotor has a diameter of <inline-formula> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$600 {\mu }\text{m}$ </tex-math></inline-formula> and is <inline-formula> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$2.5 {\mu }\text{m}$ </tex-math></inline-formula> thick. The micromotor was fabricated using a commercial three-layer polysilicon surface micro-machining process (PolyMUMPs) and the micro-polyhedrons were fabricated using a commercial bulk micro-machining process (PiezeoMUMPs). After fabrication of the components, the micro-scanner was assembled and operated under atmospheric conditions using a three-phase square wave excitation ranging from 0 V to 200 V and achieved rotational speeds of up to 2100 rpm. An optical laser beam with a wavelength of 632 nm was reflected off the sidewall of the rotating micro-polyhedron, achieving an experimentally measured scanning angular range of 57.88°, an angular scan rate of 220 radians per second and a scan speed of 25,200 lines per minute or 420 lines per second with a 12 sided micro-mirror. The ratio of the output power over the input optical power is measured over a scanning range of 22°, which is limited by the size of the photo-detector, yielding a ratio spanning from 0.18 to 0.22. This rotary micro-scanner can provide high scanning speeds and a wide scanning field of view with a footprint of 1.25 mm<sup>2</sup> and a thickness of 0.83 mm, which is suitable to implement chip-level high-performance micro-beam steering systems for various applications. Abstract:
A novel visual 3D reconstruction system, composed of a two-axis galvanometer scanner, a camera with a lens, and a set of control units, is introduced in this paper. By changing the mirror angles of the galvanometer scanner fixed in front of the camera, the boresight of the camera can be quickly adjusted. With the variable boresight, the camera can serve as a virtual multi-ocular system (VMOS), which captures the object at different perspectives. The working mechanism with a definite physical meaning is presented. A simple and efficient method for calibrating the intrinsic and extrinsic parameters of the VMOS is presented. The applicability of the proposed system for 3D reconstruction is investigated. Owing to the multiple virtual poses of the camera, the VMOS can provide stronger constraints in the object pose estimation than an ordinary perspective camera does. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed VMOS is able to achieve 3D reconstruction performance competitive with that of a conventional stereovision system with a much more concise hardware configuration.

The excerpt describes cross-threading as an abnormal jointing condition caused or revealed by uncertainty in the sensors and mechanical system. In robotic tightening, detection is based primarily on monitoring torque and/or rotational angle during operation. For high-accuracy applications, the reported method is torque-rate monitoring: torque is sampled after each specified angular increment, and the current torque-rate deviation is compared with a tolerance zone derived from the desired torque/angle curve. A deviation outside that zone is used to identify abnormal tightening behavior, which can include cross-threading, jamming, or slippage. Automatic tightening devices may also provide false-torque detection, self-diagnosis, and alarm outputs based on torque/angle sensor feedback. However, the excerpt does not give a detailed torque-angle waveform or explicit numerical signature that uniquely distinguishes cross-threading from normal thread engagement. It also does not report a specific cross-threading detection accuracy, detection rate, sampling rate, or false-alarm rate. It cautions that torque/angle sensing data can be unstable because of the dynamic tightening process, motivating intelligent controllers for more reliable fault detection. The cited 10% torque-to-clamping-force conversion and 25–30% fit-torque range concern tightening process parameters, not cross-threading detection rates or signatures.

messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-00)

| Step | Cobot Feasibility | Key Challenges | Recommended Assignment |
|---|---|---|---|
| Unpacking deliveries | Low | Unknown box geometry, straps and film, clutter, hidden or fragile contents, variable grasp points, and pose estimation; robots remain sensitive to object and pose variation (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000047) | **Shared — change plan.** Person opens packages and resolves exceptions; robots move standardized totes and known parts to inspection or kitting stations. |
| Sawing bar stock | Medium | Requires a guarded automatic saw, stock feeder, positive stops, chip control, and safe machine interface; loose long stock is awkward for a mobile cobot. | **Shared — change plan.** Person stages long/heavy stock and sets the first cut; robot can load short standardized blanks and unload cut pieces after validation. |
| CNC mill loading/unloading, ordinary parts | High | Chips or coolant on jaws and datums, part orientation, door/chuck interlocks, tool clearance, and verification that the workpiece is fully seated; mobile tending remains largely prototype-level when the environment is not tightly structured (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000033, pqac-00000038) | **Robot with human setup — retain plan.** Automate repeat loads only after CAM, first article, fixture setup, and a proven cleaning/seating routine. |
| CNC mill loading/unloading, 34.7 kg plate | Not Feasible | Plate exceeds the two arms’ combined nominal 25 kg payload before grippers, vacuum tooling, load sharing uncertainty, dynamics, and safety margin; coordinated mobile bases are not a certified lifting device. | **Human with rated vacuum lifter — retain plan.** Do not attempt dual-arm lifting; use a hoist, lifter, or higher-payload industrial robot. |
| CNC lathe loading/unloading | High | Chuck cleanliness, jaw engagement, bar protrusion, part ejection, slippery coolant-covered parts, and confirmation of clamp state. | **Robot with human setup — retain plan.** Use chuck confirmation, force-monitored insertion, part-present sensing, and periodic human inspection. |
| Deburring | Medium | Burr location and size vary; compliant tooling can miss edges or alter critical sealing surfaces, threads, and precision bores. Force-based processes add tooling and commissioning complexity (pqac-00000051) | **Shared — change plan.** Robot only repeatable external edges with compliant tools; person handles one-off internal features, sealing lands, threads, and final tactile inspection. |
| Ultrasonic washing | High | Basket loading, liquid carryover, drying, contamination control, and chemical exposure; process must be enclosed and interlocked. | **Robot — retain plan.** Use standardized perforated baskets, drip dwell, rinse/dry stations, and presence checks. |
| Measuring and inspection with machine-readable instruments | Medium | Reliable datum seating, probe access, calibration, temperature, part identification, and interpreting unexpected results; perception and sensor robustness remain deployment barriers (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000047) | **Shared — change plan.** Robot can operate digital calipers, height probes, vision, or a gauging fixture; person owns the inspection plan, calibration, ambiguous readings, and first-article disposition. |
| Kitting parts onto the long table | High | Long-table reach requires multiple docks; kit verification, small-part singulation, and preventing wrong-part placement. Fiducial or station calibration can reduce mobile-position error substantially, but task-level local sensing remains necessary (pqac-00000034, pqac-00000035) | **Robot — retain plan.** Use compartmented trays, barcodes or vision, AprilTag registration, and a weight or vision completeness check. |
| FKM O-rings in open face glands | Medium | Elastomer variability, lubrication, stretch control, twist, incomplete seating, and weak visual contrast. | **Robot after development — retain only conditionally.** Dedicated expanding mandrel or ring-loader plus 360° post-install inspection is credible; keep a person for exceptions and leak-critical acceptance. |
| FKM O-rings in half-dovetail grooves | Low | The ring must be stretched, rolled under the retaining lip, and seated without shaving or twist; force alone does not prove correct circumferential seating. | **Shared — change plan.** Treat as a development task, not assumed production capability; robot may install with a custom roller, but require human inspection or validated full-circumference machine vision. |
| FKM O-rings in internal rod-gland grooves | Low | Occluded groove, restricted tool access, risk of cutting, twist or partial seating, and difficult inspection. | **Human initially — change plan.** Automate only after a dedicated insertion cartridge or mandrel and borescope inspection demonstrate high reliability on representative glands. |
| M3–M6 stainless screws with straight nutrunner | High | Screw presentation, bit engagement, hole localization, stainless galling, cross-threading, torque scatter, and dropped screws. Torque–angle windows and torque-rate monitoring detect abnormal tightening, but require teaching and validation; reported general fault-recognition results are about 90–97%, not zero-defect assurance (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000039, pqac-00000040) | **Robot — retain plan.** Use captive or vacuum-fed screws, low-speed thread start, axial compliance, reverse-to-find-thread, torque–angle trace storage, lubrication or approved anti-seize, and human review of rejects. |
| M3–M6 stainless screws with angle-head nutrunner | Medium | Restricted access, reaction torque, tool-body collision, visibility, bit alignment, and reduced ability to recover from a bad start. | **Shared — change plan.** Automate only accessible, well-fixtured locations; redesign for straight access where possible and leave obstructed fasteners to a person. |
| Dowel pins | High | Tight alignment, chamfer condition, incorrect pin length, excessive insertion force, and false seating. Force/torque search and compliant peg-in-hole methods are established for structured assembly (pqac-00000025) | **Robot — retain plan.** Use force-limited spiral search and verify final depth plus force–displacement signature. Use a press for true interference fits. |
| Helical inserts | Medium | Tang pickup, insert compression, pitch following, cross-threading, depth control, and tang break/removal verification. | **Shared — change plan.** Robot can install repetitive inserts with a dedicated driver; person verifies threads, depth, tang removal, and repairs failures. |
| Bearings | Medium | Must press on the correct race, maintain squareness, control force, protect cleanliness, and distinguish seating from jamming. | **Shared — change plan.** Robot transfers and starts bearings; a guided instrumented press performs insertion and records force–displacement. Person handles high-value or ambiguous fits. |
| Ball screw and linear rail | Medium | Long flexible components, contamination, alignment, rail straightness, staged tightening, preload, and risk of damaging ball circuits or wipers. | **Shared — change plan.** Robots can place rails and drive accessible screws in sequence; person aligns, indicates, checks smoothness/preload, and handles the ball screw installation. |
| Cartridge heaters and thermocouples | Medium | Fragile leads, bore fit, thermal compound, bend-radius control, retention, polarity/type identification, and subsequent cable routing. | **Shared — change plan.** Robot may insert rigid cartridges and probes into clean, chamfered bores; person routes and terminates leads and verifies continuity and insulation. |
| Optics: galvo scan head placement | Medium | Cleanliness, mass properties, connector protection, precision datums, optical alignment, and calibration; scanner performance depends on machine-specific assembly and optical errors (pqac-00000045) | **Shared — change plan.** Robot may transfer and bolt a capped scan head onto kinematic datums; person performs cleanliness inspection, optical alignment, calibration, and acceptance. |
| Optics: f-theta lens on M85 thread | Low | Expensive fragile optic, contamination, fine-thread start, large threaded diameter, uncertain starting phase, cross-threading, galling or binding, and torque without damaging the lens. | **Human — change plan.** Install in a clean area with purpose-made support and torque method; robotic installation is unjustified for one unit unless the lens cartridge is redesigned with lead-ins and error-proofing. |
| Cable, hose, and fibre routing | Low | Deformable objects have high configuration uncertainty, occlusion, snagging, connector handling, bend-radius and tension constraints. Robots can route known cables through known clips with tactile sensing, but general 3-D routing remains an open problem (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021) | **Human — retain plan.** Robots may preform, present, or clip simple harness segments, but a person should route the one-off hoses, fibres, and cables. |
| TIG welding thin-wall 316L tube to flanges | Low | Joint fit-up, purge quality, distortion, arc-length and heat-input control, seam tracking, shielding, fume extraction, welding qualification, and fire hazards. In HMLV practice, programming burden can make even technically suitable cobot welding uneconomic (pqac-00000032) | **Skilled human welder — retain plan.** A one-off qualified weld is not a sensible first cobot-welding application. |
| Reading bore gauges and height gauges | Medium | Correct rocking or sweeping technique, consistent contact force, datum cleanliness, calibration, and interpretation of unstable readings. | **Human for present build — retain plan.** Automation is possible with digital gauges and dedicated fixtures, but commissioning it for one machine is unlikely to repay the effort. |
| Threading small fittings with tubes attached | Low | Flexible tube reaction, uncertain starting phase, cross-threading, wrench access, sealant control, tube twist, and inability to distinguish galling from normal tightening reliably. | **Human — retain plan.** Robot may hold or present components, but a person should start threads, control tube orientation, and make the final connection. |
| Felt-and-PTFE bore seal | Low | Soft, easily creased or damaged layers, hidden seating, friction, overlapping or split-joint control, and poor force signature. | **Human — retain plan.** Purpose-built tooling could automate a repeated design, but one-off commissioning and inspection are disproportionate. |
| Final integration: 84 kg process module onto tray | Not Feasible | Far beyond combined cobot payload; suspended-load, crush, pinch, alignment, and mobile-base stability hazards. | **Person directing a rated hoist — retain plan.** Robots may observe fiducials or guide alignment only if they never support or enter beneath the suspended load. |

### Artifact (ID artifact-01)

| Failure Mode | Severity (High/Medium/Low) | Detection Method | Mitigation Strategy |
|---|---|---|---|
| AMR docking or station-positioning error | High | Verify the AprilTag pose, reprojection residual, tag count and station transform before every manipulation; probe three or more fixed station datums with the wrist tool; reject transforms outside a validated covariance envelope. SLAM-only errors of 50–100 mm have been reported, versus ≤10 mm with ARTags; calibrated station referencing has achieved approximately ±0.12 mm in a structured example (pqac-00000034, pqac-00000035). | Use positive mechanical docking or wheel brakes, guarded fiducials, redundant tags, local datum probing and a station-specific transform—not AMR pose alone. Permit only slow free-space motion until registration passes; abort and redock on disagreement between vision and touch-off results. |
| Chips or coolant contaminating fixtures or parts | High | Dedicated close-up vision of jaws and datums; air-pressure/flow monitoring; force–displacement signature during seating; fixture gap, vacuum or part-present sensors; inspect the first part after every intervention. | Add chip-resistant jaws and datum geometry, directed air blast or wash/dry cycles, coolant-compatible grippers and protected optics. Require a clean–inspect–load–seat–verify sequence; route exceptions to a person rather than repeating a forceful insertion. |
| Part pose error in the gripper or fixture | High | Wrist-camera pose estimate immediately after pickup and again before insertion; gripper-width or jaw-position check; mass/vacuum confirmation; force-controlled guarded approach. Robotic deployment remains sensitive to object and pose variation, and force/torque data should be interpreted relative to part geometry (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000045). | Use keyed nests, asymmetrical grasp features, hard stops, poka-yoke fixtures and constrained part presentation. Regrasp or reject if independent vision and gripper-state estimates disagree; never compensate for a large pose error by forcing the part into place. |
| Cross-threading of stainless screws | High | Record torque versus angle from initial engagement onward; flag early torque rise, insufficient free-run angle, abnormal torque rate or a trace outside the taught envelope. General screwdriving-fault classifiers report roughly 90–97% recognition, but this is not zero-defect assurance (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000040). | Use chamfered holes, axial compliance, low-speed thread start and a reverse rotation to locate the thread lead. Stop at a low snug-torque threshold, back out and retry only once; quarantine repeated failures for manual thread inspection. |
| Galling of stainless-steel fasteners | High | Detect a rapid or irregular torque increase before expected seating angle, stick–slip in the torque trace, abnormal tool current or heat, and failure to back out at low reverse torque. Torque-only inference is uncertain because friction can cause errors approaching 50% (pqac-00000008). | Use compatible fastener grades/coatings, approved anti-seize or pre-applied lubricant, clean threads and slow driving speed. Avoid prevailing-torque hardware unless validated; define conservative torque–angle windows and discard—not reuse—any suspect screw or threaded component. |
| Dropped part or screw | High | Gripper-position, vacuum and pressure switches; load or wrist-force check after pickup; downward-looking vision over the transfer path; tray weight or receiving-nest part-present sensor. Threaded-part insertion experiments show that a poorly aligned part can hang insecurely and fall on release (pqac-00000025). | Use fail-safe normally closed gripping where practical, dual vacuum channels with check valves, retained or captive screws, minimum safe grip margins and low transfer heights. Provide catch trays and exclusion zones; stop the cell and reconcile inventory after every detected drop. |
| O-ring twist, cut or incomplete seating | High | Full-circumference machine vision or borescope inspection for continuity, protrusion and surface damage; compare installation force and tool travel with validated envelopes; perform leak or pressure-decay testing after closure. Force alone cannot prove untwisted seating in an occluded groove. | Control lubrication, ring orientation, stretch and insertion speed; use dedicated expanding mandrels, rollers or installation cartridges with rounded edges. Require validated automated inspection for open glands and human borescope inspection for half-dovetail or internal rod glands until process capability is demonstrated. |
| Fixture or vise seating failure | High | Verify clamp-state signal and commanded pressure; measure part-to-datum gap with displacement, proximity or vision sensing; compare insertion force–travel and work-offset probing with a golden cycle; monitor the first machining cut for anomalous load. | Clean and inspect datums before every load; use chip-shedding fixture geometry, positive locating pins, controlled clamping and redundant part-present sensing. Do not start the CNC from the clamp signal alone; require independent seating confirmation. |
| Tool breakage or severe wear during machining | High | CNC spindle-load and axis-current limits, acoustic-emission or vibration monitoring, tool-length probing after critical operations, in-process probing and dimensional checks; monitor coolant flow and machine alarms. | Retain human CAM, tooling and first-article approval; use conservative parameters, sister tools, tool-life counters and mandatory probing after high-risk cuts. Interlock unloading until the machining cycle and tool-integrity checks both pass. |
| Robot collision with CNC, fixture or workpiece | High | Safety-rated joint torque or force limits, independent safe-position or envelope monitoring, CNC door/chuck/spindle interlocks and guarded low-speed approach; validate stopping performance throughout the workspace. System-level integration and combined mobile-platform/manipulator hazards must be assessed, rather than treating the arm and base separately (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016). | Define station-specific safe corridors and forbidden zones; mechanically stabilize the base, verify registration before entering the machine and use reduced speed near hard structures. Apply safety-rated monitored stop or speed-and-separation monitoring where people can enter; perform recovery only under controlled manual mode. |
| Optics contamination or handling damage | High | Inspect capped components and mounting surfaces under controlled illumination; particle, fluorescence or dark-field inspection where justified; monitor gripper force and verify protective caps remain present until final installation. | Keep optics in sealed trays and assemble in a clean enclosure using non-shedding tooling, gloves and filtered air. Have a person perform final cleanliness acceptance, M85 lens threading, optical alignment and galvo calibration because scanner performance is sensitive to assembly-specific optical and mechanical errors. |
| Wrong part picked or assembled | High | Barcode, Data Matrix or RFID identity check at source and destination; vision confirmation of geometry and orientation; kit-tray weight/completeness check; recipe-to-part-number interlock and fastener-count reconciliation. Reliable object recognition and coordination remain manufacturing-robot deployment barriers (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000047). | Use one-part-per-pocket kits, uniquely keyed nests, segregated fastener feeders and electronic work instructions tied to the serial-number build record. Require two independent identifiers for look-alike or safety-critical parts and stop for human disposition on any mismatch. |

{"answer": "# Critical Review: Two Mobile Manipulators Building a Desktop LPBF Machine in a University Shop

## 1. Published Examples and Industrial Practice of Mobile Manipulators for CNC Machine Tending and Assembly

### 1.1 Maturity of Mobile-Manipulator Machine Tending

Autonomous mobile manipulators (AMMs) combining an AMR base with a cobot arm are recognized as a scalable solution for high-mix, low-volume CNC tending, but the published evidence base remains largely at the prototype or conceptual level (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000003). A systematic review of robotic machine-tending literature found that AMM-based loading and unloading using 3D point-cloud object detection, marker recognition, and CNN-based material handling are classified as prototypes, with no fully autonomous system yet replacing a human for tasks such as cycle start, emergency handling, or screen-based machine interaction (pqac-00000002). One cited example uses a KUKA AMR with a gripper and vision on the end-effector to pick raw material from local storage and transport it to a machine for loading, but this remains a demonstration rather than a production deployment (pqac-00000038).

### 1.2 Achieved Positioning Accuracy After Docking and Re-Registration

Positioning accuracy is the principal bottleneck for mobile manipulation. SLAM-only AMR navigation produces positioning errors of approximately 50–100 mm (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000035). Adding fiducial markers (ARTags) together with a wrist-mounted vision system reduces errors to 10 mm or less, representing an improvement of more than 80% (pqac-00000000). Vision-based compensation in one study achieved an average offset of 0.19 mm (pqac-00000035). In a robotic-chemist application where a touch-sensitive six-point station calibration was used, positioning accuracy improved to ±0.12 mm with ±0.005° orientation over 563 movements (pqac-00000034). The KUKA KMR iiwa has a manufacturer-quoted positioning accuracy of up to ±5 mm, with experimental results at low speed generally remaining below 2 mm (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000037). Your proposed ±3 mm AMR docking plus AprilTag re-registration with a wrist camera is therefore realistic and consistent with published results, provided that station-specific datum probing or touch-off is added as a secondary verification. For CNC loading at ±0.1 mm repeatability, the cobot's own repeatability (±0.05 mm for UR10e/12e) must be used relative to a station-registered frame, not the AMR pose.

### 1.3 Uptime, Failure Rates, and Cycle-Time Penalties

No published study reports operational uptime, mean-time-between-failure, or quantified cycle-time penalties for a mobile manipulator tending CNC machines in production. NIST's survey of manufacturing robotics barriers identified organizational uptime targets of 16,000–80,000 hours and noted that uncertainty about robotic reliability is a major adoption barrier (pqac-00000044). The docking overhead per station visit—including navigation, docking, registration verification, and tool change—is an inherent cycle-time penalty, estimated at 1–3 minutes per station visit based on AMR transit speeds and typical registration sequences, which is significant for short machining cycles but negligible for multi-hour CNC operations.

### 1.4 Commissioning Effort Per New Task

Cobot manufacturers claim that a simple screwdriving or pick-and-place task can be programmed in minutes, while conventional automation deployment commonly takes 8–17 weeks (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000042, pqac-00000043). However, full cell commissioning—including safety assessment, sensing, grippers, recovery logic, and validation—is substantially longer and is not well-quantified in the literature. In one case study of cobot welding for an SME, only about 3% of technically suitable welding jobs were actually automated because programming time was burdensome for small batches, even though 95% of jobs were theoretically feasible (pqac-00000032). NIST identifies long integration timelines, programming burden, and limited redeployability as persistent barriers to manufacturing robot adoption, particularly in high-mix production (pqac-00000044, pqac-00000045, pqac-00000046, pqac-00000050).

### 1.5 What Still Needs People

Published reviews consistently identify the following as requiring human involvement: emergency handling and machine-screen interaction for CNC cycle control (pqac-00000002); first-article verification, CAM programming, and tool setting; heavy-part handling beyond cobot payload; deformable-object manipulation (cables, hoses); exception handling and fault recovery; inspection requiring judgment; and process changes or new part introductions (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000051).

---

## 2. Step-by-Step Feasibility Assessment and Evaluation of the Person-Only List

The following table provides a detailed assessment of each proposed step, its feasibility for present-day cobots, and whether the current plan's assignment is correct or should be changed.

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

### 2.1 Assessment of Your Person-Only List

Your person-only list is **mostly correct but slightly too short**. The following items should be added or reconsidered:

**Items correctly kept manual:**
- Loading the 34.7 kg plate (exceeds payload)
- CAM and first-article runs
- Tool setting
- TIG welding thin-wall 316L
- Reading bore and height gauges (for one-off)
- Routing hoses, fibres, and cables (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000024)
- Threading small fittings with tubes attached
- Installing the felt-and-PTFE bore seal
- Lifting anything over combined payload (84 kg module)

**Items that should be added to the person-only or person-shared list:**
- **F-theta lens installation (M85 thread):** The f-theta lens is an expensive, fragile optic on a large fine thread. Cross-threading risk, contamination risk, and uncertain thread engagement make robotic installation inadvisable for one unit.
- **Internal rod-gland O-rings:** Occluded grooves with restricted access and difficult inspection should start as human tasks.
- **Half-dovetail groove O-rings:** The ring must be stretched under retaining lips; keep human inspection until validated.
- **Optics alignment and calibration:** Galvo scan head calibration is machine-specific and sensitive to assembly defects (pqac-00000045).
- **Ball screw installation:** Protecting ball circuits, controlling preload, and assessing smoothness are judgment-intensive.
- **Deburring of precision sealing surfaces and threads:** Compliant robotic deburring is feasible for external edges but not for one-off critical internal features.

**Items where dual-arm lifting (15–35 kg as a pair) may be cautiously feasible:**
Two UR12e arms on separate MiR250 bases could theoretically share a 15–25 kg load (each arm lifting 7.5–12.5 kg including tooling), but this requires coordinated dual-mobile-base control, which has no published safety standard or industrial precedent. For a university shop, the safer approach is to use a rated lifting device (vacuum lifter, hoist, or jib crane) for any part above approximately 10 kg and reserve dual-arm coordination for holding and orienting lighter components.

---

## 3. Hardest Failure Modes and Detection Methods

The following table summarizes the most critical failure modes for your proposed cell, along with detection and mitigation strategies.

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

### 3.1 Detailed Discussion of Key Failure Modes

**Cross-threading and galling of stainless screws** are the highest-consequence assembly failures. Cross-threading occurs when external and internal threads engage on misaligned helices (pqac-00000041). Detection relies on torque–angle monitoring: each successful screw insertion produces a characteristic torque–angle signature, and deviations outside a taught window indicate faults. Torque-rate monitoring samples torque after each angular increment and compares the current deviation against a tolerance zone (pqac-00000040). Published general fault-recognition rates reach approximately 90–97% using teach-based, ANN, or ML classifiers, but deployment-ready performance on actual assembly lines remains an ongoing challenge (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000026). Torque-only control can deviate by up to 50% due to friction, making it unsuitable for precise fault detection without supplementary angle data (pqac-00000008).

Galling is a specific risk for stainless steel that is **not addressed in the robotic assembly literature**. It requires process-level mitigation: compatible alloy grades, anti-seize lubricant, clean threads, slow driving speed, and conservative torque limits. The torque signature for galling—a sudden, irregular torque increase with stick-slip behavior—overlaps with other friction anomalies, making automated detection unreliable without validated process-specific envelopes.

**Chips and coolant contamination** of fixtures and datums is the most common CNC machine-tending failure mode. Swarf on a vise jaw or chuck datum creates a seating error that propagates through machining. Detection requires dedicated close-up vision of datum surfaces, air-pressure/flow confirmation, and force-displacement monitoring during part seating.

**Part pose errors** from gripper misalignment or incorrect orientation cause downstream failures in CNC loading and assembly. Force/torque data during insertion show distinctive profiles—sawtooth patterns during successful threading, and distinctive force spikes or stalls during failures—but relating force/torque data to part geometry is identified as a missing capability (pqac-00000025).

**O-ring twist and incomplete seating** are especially dangerous for half-dovetail and internal rod glands where the groove is occluded. Our current plan keeps a person for: loading a 34.7 kg aluminium plate blank onto the mill with a vacuum tube lifter, CAM and first-article runs, tool setting, TIG welding a thin-wall 316L tube to flanges, reading bore and height gauges, routing hoses, fibres and cables, threading small fittings with tubes attached, installing a felt-and-PTFE bore seal, and lifting anything over the arms' combined payload.

Please review this plan critically, with sources: (1) published examples and industrial practice of mobile manipulators (AMR plus cobot) tending CNC machines and doing assembly in high-mix, low-volume or one-off settings: achieved positioning accuracy after docking and re-registration, uptime and failure rates, cycle-time penalties, commissioning effort per new task, and what still needed people; (2) which of the steps above are realistic for cobots today and which are not, and whether our person-only list is too long or too short (for example: can cobots route cables and hoses, install felt seals, TIG weld one-off parts, read bore gauges, thread fittings with tubing attached, handle 15-35 kg plates as a pair); (3) the hardest failure modes to expect (chips and coolant, fixture seating, part pose errors, cross-threading and galling of stainless screws, dropping parts, O-ring twist), and how they are detected; (4) safety for a shop where people and mobile manipulators work together: ISO 10218-1/-2 (2025), ISO/TS 15066, ANSI/A3 R15.08 for industrial mobile robots, and what a risk assessment for this cell would need; (5) a realistic estimate of the person-hours and calendar time to commission such a cell for one machine compared with simply building it by hand. Give concrete numbers where they exist and say clearly where you are estimating.
answer.answer:
# Critical Review: Two Mobile Manipulators Building a Desktop LPBF Machine in a University Shop

## 1. Published Examples and Industrial Practice of Mobile Manipulators for CNC Machine Tending and Assembly

### 1.1 Maturity of Mobile-Manipulator Machine Tending

Autonomous mobile manipulators (AMMs) combining an AMR base with a cobot arm are recognized as a scalable solution for high-mix, low-volume CNC tending, but the published evidence base remains largely at the prototype or conceptual level (feiyu2024anintelligentframework pages 43-47, khishtan2026areviewof pages 2-4). A systematic review of robotic machine-tending literature found that AMM-based loading and unloading using 3D point-cloud object detection, marker recognition, and CNN-based material handling are classified as prototypes, with no fully autonomous system yet replacing a human for tasks such as cycle start, emergency handling, or screen-based machine interaction (feiyu2024anintelligentframework pages 43-47). One cited example uses a KUKA AMR with a gripper and vision on the end-effector to pick raw material from local storage and transport it to a machine for loading, but this remains a demonstration rather than a production deployment (feiyu2024anintelligentframework pages 43-47).

### 1.2 Achieved Positioning Accuracy After Docking and Re-Registration

Positioning accuracy is the principal bottleneck for mobile manipulation. SLAM-only AMR navigation produces positioning errors of approximately 50–100 mm (hifi2025flexibleandintelligent pages 74-80). Adding fiducial markers (ARTags) together with a wrist-mounted vision system reduces errors to 10 mm or less, representing an improvement of more than 80% (hifi2025flexibleandintelligent pages 74-80). Vision-based compensation in one study achieved an average offset of 0.19 mm (hifi2025flexibleandintelligent pages 74-80). In a robotic-chemist application where a touch-sensitive six-point station calibration was used, positioning accuracy improved to ±0.12 mm with ±0.005° orientation over 563 movements (hifi2025flexibleandintelligent pages 69-74). The KUKA KMR iiwa has a manufacturer-quoted positioning accuracy of up to ±5 mm, with experimental results at low speed generally remaining below 2 mm (hifi2025flexibleandintelligent pages 208-214, hifi2025flexibleandintelligent pages 63-69). Your proposed ±3 mm AMR docking plus AprilTag re-registration with a wrist camera is therefore realistic and consistent with published results, provided that station-specific datum probing or touch-off is added as a secondary verification. For CNC loading at ±0.1 mm repeatability, the cobot's own repeatability (±0.05 mm for UR10e/12e) must be used relative to a station-registered frame, not the AMR pose.

### 1.3 Uptime, Failure Rates, and Cycle-Time Penalties

No published study reports operational uptime, mean-time-between-failure, or quantified cycle-time penalties for a mobile manipulator tending CNC machines in production. NIST's survey of manufacturing robotics barriers identified organizational uptime targets of 16,000–80,000 hours and noted that uncertainty about robotic reliability is a major adoption barrier (messina2024researchopportunitiesfor pages 17-20). The docking overhead per station visit—including navigation, docking, registration verification, and tool change—is an inherent cycle-time penalty, estimated at 1–3 minutes per station visit based on AMR transit speeds and typical registration sequences, which is significant for short machining cycles but negligible for multi-hour CNC operations.

### 1.4 Commissioning Effort Per New Task

Cobot manufacturers claim that a simple screwdriving or pick-and-place task can be programmed in minutes, while conventional automation deployment commonly takes 8–17 weeks (brera2022collaborativescrewdrivingintegrating pages 35-38, brera2022collaborativescrewdrivingintegratinga pages 35-38). However, full cell commissioning—including safety assessment, sensing, grippers, recovery logic, and validation—is substantially longer and is not well-quantified in the literature. In one case study of cobot welding for an SME, only about 3% of technically suitable welding jobs were actually automated because programming time was burdensome for small batches, even though 95% of jobs were theoretically feasible (schumacher2022technologyadoptionof pages 5-7). NIST identifies long integration timelines, programming burden, and limited redeployability as persistent barriers to manufacturing robot adoption, particularly in high-mix production (messina2024researchopportunitiesfor pages 17-20, messina2024researchopportunitiesfor pages 34-37, messina2024researchopportunitiesfor pages 13-17, messina2024researchopportunitiesfor pages 20-25).

### 1.5 What Still Needs People

Published reviews consistently identify the following as requiring human involvement: emergency handling and machine-screen interaction for CNC cycle control (feiyu2024anintelligentframework pages 43-47); first-article verification, CAM programming, and tool setting; heavy-part handling beyond cobot payload; deformable-object manipulation (cables, hoses); exception handling and fault recovery; inspection requiring judgment; and process changes or new part introductions (messina2024researchopportunitiesfor pages 34-37, messina2024researchopportunitiesfor pages 28-30).

---

## 2. Step-by-Step Feasibility Assessment and Evaluation of the Person-Only List

The following table provides a detailed assessment of each proposed step, its feasibility for present-day cobots, and whether the current plan's assignment is correct or should be changed.

| Step | Cobot Feasibility | Key Challenges | Recommended Assignment |
|---|---|---|---|
| Unpacking deliveries | Low | Unknown box geometry, straps and film, clutter, hidden or fragile contents, variable grasp points, and pose estimation; robots remain sensitive to object and pose variation (messina2024researchopportunitiesfor pages 34-37, messina2024researchopportunitiesfor pages 39-42) | **Shared — change plan.** Person opens packages and resolves exceptions; robots move standardized totes and known parts to inspection or kitting stations. |
| Sawing bar stock | Medium | Requires a guarded automatic saw, stock feeder, positive stops, chip control, and safe machine interface; loose long stock is awkward for a mobile cobot. | **Shared — change plan.** Person stages long/heavy stock and sets the first cut; robot can load short standardized blanks and unload cut pieces after validation. |
| CNC mill loading/unloading, ordinary parts | High | Chips or coolant on jaws and datums, part orientation, door/chuck interlocks, tool clearance, and verification that the workpiece is fully seated; mobile tending remains largely prototype-level when the environment is not tightly structured (feiyu2024anintelligentframework pages 43-47, feiyu2024anintelligentframework pages 47-52) | **Robot with human setup — retain plan.** Automate repeat loads only after CAM, first article, fixture setup, and a proven cleaning/seating routine. |
| CNC mill loading/unloading, 34.7 kg plate | Not Feasible | Plate exceeds the two arms’ combined nominal 25 kg payload before grippers, vacuum tooling, load sharing uncertainty, dynamics, and safety margin; coordinated mobile bases are not a certified lifting device. | **Human with rated vacuum lifter — retain plan.** Do not attempt dual-arm lifting; use a hoist, lifter, or higher-payload industrial robot. |
| CNC lathe loading/unloading | High | Chuck cleanliness, jaw engagement, bar protrusion, part ejection, slippery coolant-covered parts, and confirmation of clamp state. | **Robot with human setup — retain plan.** Use chuck confirmation, force-monitored insertion, part-present sensing, and periodic human inspection. |
| Deburring | Medium | Burr location and size vary; compliant tooling can miss edges or alter critical sealing surfaces, threads, and precision bores. Force-based processes add tooling and commissioning complexity (messina2024researchopportunitiesfor pages 28-30) | **Shared — change plan.** Robot only repeatable external edges with compliant tools; person handles one-off internal features, sealing lands, threads, and final tactile inspection. |
| Ultrasonic washing | High | Basket loading, liquid carryover, drying, contamination control, and chemical exposure; process must be enclosed and interlocked. | **Robot — retain plan.** Use standardized perforated baskets, drip dwell, rinse/dry stations, and presence checks. |
| Measuring and inspection with machine-readable instruments | Medium | Reliable datum seating, probe access, calibration, temperature, part identification, and interpreting unexpected results; perception and sensor robustness remain deployment barriers (messina2024researchopportunitiesfor pages 34-37, messina2024researchopportunitiesfor pages 39-42) | **Shared — change plan.** Robot can operate digital calipers, height probes, vision, or a gauging fixture; person owns the inspection plan, calibration, ambiguous readings, and first-article disposition. |
| Kitting parts onto the long table | High | Long-table reach requires multiple docks; kit verification, small-part singulation, and preventing wrong-part placement. Fiducial or station calibration can reduce mobile-position error substantially, but task-level local sensing remains necessary (hifi2025flexibleandintelligent pages 69-74, hifi2025flexibleandintelligent pages 74-80) | **Robot — retain plan.** Use compartmented trays, barcodes or vision, AprilTag registration, and a weight or vision completeness check. |
| FKM O-rings in open face glands | Medium | Elastomer variability, lubrication, stretch control, twist, incomplete seating, and weak visual contrast. | **Robot after development — retain only conditionally.** Dedicated expanding mandrel or ring-loader plus 360° post-install inspection is credible; keep a person for exceptions and leak-critical acceptance. |
| FKM O-rings in half-dovetail grooves | Low | The ring must be stretched, rolled under the retaining lip, and seated without shaving or twist; force alone does not prove correct circumferential seating. | **Shared — change plan.** Treat as a development task, not assumed production capability; robot may install with a custom roller, but require human inspection or validated full-circumference machine vision. |
| FKM O-rings in internal rod-gland grooves | Low | Occluded groove, restricted tool access, risk of cutting, twist or partial seating, and difficult inspection. | **Human initially — change plan.** Automate only after a dedicated insertion cartridge or mandrel and borescope inspection demonstrate high reliability on representative glands. |
| M3–M6 stainless screws with straight nutrunner | High | Screw presentation, bit engagement, hole localization, stainless galling, cross-threading, torque scatter, and dropped screws. Torque–angle windows and torque-rate monitoring detect abnormal tightening, but require teaching and validation; reported general fault-recognition results are about 90–97%, not zero-defect assurance (brera2022collaborativescrewdrivingintegrating pages 31-35, xu2019areviewon pages 16-17) | **Robot — retain plan.** Use captive or vacuum-fed screws, low-speed thread start, axial compliance, reverse-to-find-thread, torque–angle trace storage, lubrication or approved anti-seize, and human review of rejects. |
| M3–M6 stainless screws with angle-head nutrunner | Medium | Restricted access, reaction torque, tool-body collision, visibility, bit alignment, and reduced ability to recover from a bad start. | **Shared — change plan.** Automate only accessible, well-fixtured locations; redesign for straight access where possible and leave obstructed fasteners to a person. |
| Dowel pins | High | Tight alignment, chamfer condition, incorrect pin length, excessive insertion force, and false seating. Force/torque search and compliant peg-in-hole methods are established for structured assembly (watson2020autonomousindustrialassembly pages 16-18) | **Robot — retain plan.** Use force-limited spiral search and verify final depth plus force–displacement signature. Use a press for true interference fits. |
| Helical inserts | Medium | Tang pickup, insert compression, pitch following, cross-threading, depth control, and tang break/removal verification. | **Shared — change plan.** Robot can install repetitive inserts with a dedicated driver; person verifies threads, depth, tang removal, and repairs failures. |
| Bearings | Medium | Must press on the correct race, maintain squareness, control force, protect cleanliness, and distinguish seating from jamming. | **Shared — change plan.** Robot transfers and starts bearings; a guided instrumented press performs insertion and records force–displacement. Person handles high-value or ambiguous fits. |
| Ball screw and linear rail | Medium | Long flexible components, contamination, alignment, rail straightness, staged tightening, preload, and risk of damaging ball circuits or wipers. | **Shared — change plan.** Robots can place rails and drive accessible screws in sequence; person aligns, indicates, checks smoothness/preload, and handles the ball screw installation. |
| Cartridge heaters and thermocouples | Medium | Fragile leads, bore fit, thermal compound, bend-radius control, retention, polarity/type identification, and subsequent cable routing. | **Shared — change plan.** Robot may insert rigid cartridges and probes into clean, chamfered bores; person routes and terminates leads and verifies continuity and insulation. |

| Cable, hose, and fibre routing | Low | Deformable objects have high configuration uncertainty, occlusion, snagging, connector handling, bend-radius and tension constraints.
