| TIG welding thin-wall 316L tube to flanges | Low | Joint fit-up, purge quality, distortion, arc-length and heat-input control, seam tracking, shielding, fume extraction, welding qualification, and fire hazards. In HMLV practice, programming burden can make even technically suitable cobot welding uneconomic (schumacher2022technologyadoptionof pages 5-7) | **Skilled human welder — retain plan.** A one-off qualified weld is not a sensible first cobot-welding application. |
| Reading bore gauges and height gauges | Medium | Correct rocking or sweeping technique, consistent contact force, datum cleanliness, calibration, and interpretation of unstable readings. | **Human for present build — retain plan.** Automation is possible with digital gauges and dedicated fixtures, but commissioning it for one machine is unlikely to repay the effort. |
| Threading small fittings with tubes attached | Low | Flexible tube reaction, uncertain starting phase, cross-threading, wrench access, sealant control, tube twist, and inability to distinguish galling from normal tightening reliably. | **Human — retain plan.** Robot may hold or present components, but a person should start threads, control tube orientation, and make the final connection. |
| Felt-and-PTFE bore seal | Low | Soft, easily creased or damaged layers, hidden seating, friction, overlapping or split-joint control, and poor force signature. | **Human — retain plan.** Purpose-built tooling could automate a repeated design, but one-off commissioning and inspection are disproportionate. |
| Final integration: 84 kg process module onto tray | Not Feasible | Far beyond combined cobot payload; suspended-load, crush, pinch, alignment, and mobile-base stability hazards. | **Person directing a rated hoist — retain plan.** Robots may observe fiducials or guide alignment only if they never support or enter beneath the suspended load. |


*Table: Step-by-step assessment of which machining and assembly operations fit present-day cobots and where human work or task redesign remains necessary. The recommendations also identify where the proposed allocation should be retained or changed.*

### 2.1 Assessment of Your Person-Only List

Your person-only list is **mostly correct but slightly too short**. The following items should be added or reconsidered:

**Items correctly kept manual:**
- Loading the 34.7 kg plate (exceeds payload)
- CAM and first-article runs
- Tool setting
- TIG welding thin-wall 316L
- Reading bore and height gauges (for one-off)
- Routing hoses, fibres, and cables (caporali2026roboticperceptionand pages 24-25, caporali2026roboticperceptionand pages 23-24, govoni2026designcontroland pages 31-34, monguzzi2023roboticmanipulationof pages 12-17)
- Threading small fittings with tubes attached
- Installing the felt-and-PTFE bore seal
- Lifting anything over combined payload (84 kg module)

**Items that should be added to the person-only or person-shared list:**
- **F-theta lens installation (M85 thread):** The f-theta lens is an expensive, fragile optic on a large fine thread. Cross-threading risk, contamination risk, and uncertain thread engagement make robotic installation inadvisable for one unit.
- **Internal rod-gland O-rings:** Occluded grooves with restricted access and difficult inspection should start as human tasks.
- **Half-dovetail groove O-rings:** The ring must be stretched under retaining lips; keep human inspection until validated.
- **Optics alignment and calibration:** Galvo scan head calibration is machine-specific and sensitive to assembly defects (messina2024researchopportunitiesfor pages 34-37).
- **Ball screw installation:** Protecting ball circuits, controlling preload, and assessing smoothness are judgment-intensive.
- **Deburring of precision sealing surfaces and threads:** Compliant robotic deburring is feasible for external edges but not for one-off critical internal features.

**Items where dual-arm lifting (15–35 kg as a pair) may be cautiously feasible:**
Two UR12e arms on separate MiR250 bases could theoretically share a 15–25 kg load (each arm lifting 7.5–12.5 kg including tooling), but this requires coordinated dual-mobile-base control, which has no published safety standard or industrial precedent. For a university shop, the safer approach is to use a rated lifting device (vacuum lifter, hoist, or jib crane) for any part above approximately 10 kg and reserve dual-arm coordination for holding and orienting lighter components.

---

## 3. Hardest Failure Modes and Detection Methods

The following table summarizes the most critical failure modes for your proposed cell, along with detection and mitigation strategies.

| Failure Mode | Severity (High/Medium/Low) | Detection Method | Mitigation Strategy |
|---|---|---|---|
| AMR docking or station-positioning error | High | Verify the AprilTag pose, reprojection residual, tag count and station transform before every manipulation; probe three or more fixed station datums with the wrist tool; reject transforms outside a validated covariance envelope. SLAM-only errors of 50–100 mm have been reported, versus ≤10 mm with ARTags; calibrated station referencing has achieved approximately ±0.12 mm in a structured example (hifi2025flexibleandintelligent pages 69-74, hifi2025flexibleandintelligent pages 74-80). | Use positive mechanical docking or wheel brakes, guarded fiducials, redundant tags, local datum probing and a station-specific transform—not AMR pose alone. Permit only slow free-space motion until registration passes; abort and redock on disagreement between vision and touch-off results. |
| Chips or coolant contaminating fixtures or parts | High | Dedicated close-up vision of jaws and datums; air-pressure/flow monitoring; force–displacement signature during seating; fixture gap, vacuum or part-present sensors; inspect the first part after every intervention. | Add chip-resistant jaws and datum geometry, directed air blast or wash/dry cycles, coolant-compatible grippers and protected optics. Require a clean–inspect–load–seat–verify sequence; route exceptions to a person rather than repeating a forceful insertion. |
| Part pose error in the gripper or fixture | High | Wrist-camera pose estimate immediately after pickup and again before insertion; gripper-width or jaw-position check; mass/vacuum confirmation; force-controlled guarded approach. Robotic deployment remains sensitive to object and pose variation, and force/torque data should be interpreted relative to part geometry (watson2020autonomousindustrialassembly pages 16-18, messina2024researchopportunitiesfor pages 34-37). | Use keyed nests, asymmetrical grasp features, hard stops, poka-yoke fixtures and constrained part presentation. Regrasp or reject if independent vision and gripper-state estimates disagree; never compensate for a large pose error by forcing the part into place. |
| Cross-threading of stainless screws | High | Record torque versus angle from initial engagement onward; flag early torque rise, insufficient free-run angle, abnormal torque rate or a trace outside the taught envelope. General screwdriving-fault classifiers report roughly 90–97% recognition, but this is not zero-defect assurance (brera2022collaborativescrewdrivingintegrating pages 31-35, xu2019areviewon pages 16-17). | Use chamfered holes, axial compliance, low-speed thread start and a reverse rotation to locate the thread lead. Stop at a low snug-torque threshold, back out and retry only once; quarantine repeated failures for manual thread inspection. |
| Galling of stainless-steel fasteners | High | Detect a rapid or irregular torque increase before expected seating angle, stick–slip in the torque trace, abnormal tool current or heat, and failure to back out at low reverse torque. Torque-only inference is uncertain because friction can cause errors approaching 50% (brera2022collaborativescrewdrivingintegrating pages 31-35). | Use compatible fastener grades/coatings, approved anti-seize or pre-applied lubricant, clean threads and slow driving speed. Avoid prevailing-torque hardware unless validated; define conservative torque–angle windows and discard—not reuse—any suspect screw or threaded component. |
| Dropped part or screw | High | Gripper-position, vacuum and pressure switches; load or wrist-force check after pickup; downward-looking vision over the transfer path; tray weight or receiving-nest part-present sensor. Threaded-part insertion experiments show that a poorly aligned part can hang insecurely and fall on release (watson2020autonomousindustrialassembly pages 16-18). | Use fail-safe normally closed gripping where practical, dual vacuum channels with check valves, retained or captive screws, minimum safe grip margins and low transfer heights. Provide catch trays and exclusion zones; stop the cell and reconcile inventory after every detected drop. |
| O-ring twist, cut or incomplete seating | High | Full-circumference machine vision or borescope inspection for continuity, protrusion and surface damage; compare installation force and tool travel with validated envelopes; perform leak or pressure-decay testing after closure. Force alone cannot prove untwisted seating in an occluded groove. | Control lubrication, ring orientation, stretch and insertion speed; use dedicated expanding mandrels, rollers or installation cartridges with rounded edges. Require validated automated inspection for open glands and human borescope inspection for half-dovetail or internal rod glands until process capability is demonstrated. |
| Fixture or vise seating failure | High | Verify clamp-state signal and commanded pressure; measure part-to-datum gap with displacement, proximity or vision sensing; compare insertion force–travel and work-offset probing with a golden cycle; monitor the first machining cut for anomalous load. | Clean and inspect datums before every load; use chip-shedding fixture geometry, positive locating pins, controlled clamping and redundant part-present sensing. Do not start the CNC from the clamp signal alone; require independent seating confirmation. |
| Tool breakage or severe wear during machining | High | CNC spindle-load and axis-current limits, acoustic-emission or vibration monitoring, tool-length probing after critical operations, in-process probing and dimensional checks; monitor coolant flow and machine alarms. | Retain human CAM, tooling and first-article approval; use conservative parameters, sister tools, tool-life counters and mandatory probing after high-risk cuts. Interlock unloading until the machining cycle and tool-integrity checks both pass. |
| Robot collision with CNC, fixture or workpiece | High | Safety-rated joint torque or force limits, independent safe-position or envelope monitoring, CNC door/chuck/spindle interlocks and guarded low-speed approach; validate stopping performance throughout the workspace. System-level integration and combined mobile-platform/manipulator hazards must be assessed, rather than treating the arm and base separately (faria2020safetyrequirementsfor pages 4-6, vitolo2022mobilerobotsand pages 5-6, alexandra2019safetyofmobile pages 2-3). | Define station-specific safe corridors and forbidden zones; mechanically stabilize the base, verify registration before entering the machine and use reduced speed near hard structures. Apply safety-rated monitored stop or speed-and-separation monitoring where people can enter; perform recovery only under controlled manual mode. |
| Optics contamination or handling damage | High | Inspect capped components and mounting surfaces under controlled illumination; particle, fluorescence or dark-field inspection where justified; monitor gripper force and verify protective caps remain present until final installation. | Keep optics in sealed trays and assemble in a clean enclosure using non-shedding tooling, gloves and filtered air. Have a person perform final cleanliness acceptance, M85 lens threading, optical alignment and galvo calibration because scanner performance is sensitive to assembly-specific optical and mechanical errors. |
| Wrong part picked or assembled | High | Barcode, Data Matrix or RFID identity check at source and destination; vision confirmation of geometry and orientation; kit-tray weight/completeness check; recipe-to-part-number interlock and fastener-count reconciliation. Reliable object recognition and coordination remain manufacturing-robot deployment barriers (messina2024researchopportunitiesfor pages 34-37, messina2024researchopportunitiesfor pages 39-42). | Use one-part-per-pocket kits, uniquely keyed nests, segregated fastener feeders and electronic work instructions tied to the serial-number build record. Require two independent identifiers for look-alike or safety-critical parts and stop for human disposition on any mismatch. |


*Table: Key failure modes for the proposed mobile-manipulator machining and assembly cell, with practical detection and mitigation controls. Severity reflects potential damage to personnel, machines, high-value components, or latent product quality.*

### 3.1 Detailed Discussion of Key Failure Modes

**Cross-threading and galling of stainless screws** are the highest-consequence assembly failures. Cross-threading occurs when external and internal threads engage on misaligned helices (pagliara2025improvingdependabilityin pages 2-3). Detection relies on torque–angle monitoring: each successful screw insertion produces a characteristic torque–angle signature, and deviations outside a taught window indicate faults. Torque-rate monitoring samples torque after each angular increment and compares the current deviation against a tolerance zone (xu2019areviewon pages 16-17). Published general fault-recognition rates reach approximately 90–97% using teach-based, ANN, or ML classifiers, but deployment-ready performance on actual assembly lines remains an ongoing challenge (brera2022collaborativescrewdrivingintegrating pages 31-35). Torque-only control can deviate by up to 50% due to friction, making it unsuitable for precise fault detection without supplementary angle data (brera2022collaborativescrewdrivingintegrating pages 31-35).

Galling is a specific risk for stainless steel that is **not addressed in the robotic assembly literature**. It requires process-level mitigation: compatible alloy grades, anti-seize lubricant, clean threads, slow driving speed, and conservative torque limits. The torque signature for galling—a sudden, irregular torque increase with stick-slip behavior—overlaps with other friction anomalies, making automated detection unreliable without validated process-specific envelopes.

**Chips and coolant contamination** of fixtures and datums is the most common CNC machine-tending failure mode. Swarf on a vise jaw or chuck datum creates a seating error that propagates through machining. Detection requires dedicated close-up vision of datum surfaces, air-pressure/flow confirmation, and force-displacement monitoring during part seating.

**Part pose errors** from gripper misalignment or incorrect orientation cause downstream failures in CNC loading and assembly. Force/torque data during insertion show distinctive profiles—sawtooth patterns during successful threading, and distinctive force spikes or stalls during failures—but relating force/torque data to part geometry is identified as a missing capability (watson2020autonomousindustrialassembly pages 16-18).

**O-ring twist and incomplete seating** are especially dangerous for half-dovetail and internal rod glands where the groove is occluded. Force alone does not prove correct circumferential seating, and visual inspection may be inadequate for internal grooves. Full-circumference machine vision, borescope inspection, or pressure-decay testing after closure are the most reliable detection methods.

---

## 4. Safety Standards and Risk Assessment Requirements

### 4.1 Applicable Standards

The safety framework for your proposed cell must combine multiple standards because no single standard covers integrated mobile manipulators (alexandra2019safetyofmobile pages 3-4, vitolo2022mobilerobotsand pages 5-6, alexandra2019safetyofmobile pages 2-3):

- **ISO 10218-1:2025** addresses robot design and construction, including functional safety, operating modes, emergency stops, and speed limiting (duplak2025applicationofsafety pages 2-4).
- **ISO 10218-2:2025** addresses robot system integration, covering cell layout, safeguarding, commissioning, programming, operation, and maintenance. The 2025 revision gives greater attention to collaborative applications (faria2020safetyrequirementsfor pages 4-6, valori2021validatingsafetyin pages 5-6).
- **ISO/TS 15066:2016** supplements ISO 10218 for collaborative operation and defines four modes: Safety-rated Monitored Stop (SRMS), Hand-Guiding (HG), Speed and Separation Monitoring (SSM), and Power and Force Limiting (PFL) (faria2020safetyrequirementsfor pages 4-6, valori2021validatingsafetyin pages 5-6, duplak2025applicationofsafety pages 4-6). PFL requires that contact forces remain below body-region-specific thresholds. For a mobile manipulator where contact with the face cannot be excluded, the worst-case transient force limit is 65 N and the corresponding maximum interface speed is 0.12 m/s (vitolo2022mobilerobotsand pages 15-17). The body model contains 29 specific contact locations grouped into 12 body regions; quasi-static limits are half the transient limits (scibilia2021analysisofinterlaboratory pages 1-2, scibilia2021analysisofinterlaboratory pages 2-3).
- **ISO 3691-4** addresses safety requirements for driverless industrial trucks, including AMRs (alexandra2019safetyofmobile pages 2-3).
- **ANSI/RIA R15.08** was developed specifically for industrial mobile robots and mobile manipulators to address gaps among AGV, AMR, and mobile-manipulator standards. At the time of key publications, it was announced for publication in early 2019 as a draft (alexandra2019safetyofmobile pages 3-4). It is now published and addresses the combined hazards of mobility and manipulation.
- **ISO 12100** provides the overarching risk-assessment methodology (mariano2026roboticsafetyin pages 3-3, duplak2025applicationofsafety pages 2-4, duplak2025applicationofsafety pages 4-6).

### 4.2 Risk Assessment Requirements for This Cell

A documented, iterative risk assessment is required covering (mariano2026roboticsafetyin pages 3-3, faria2020safetyrequirementsfor pages 4-6, duplak2025applicationofsafety pages 2-4, alexandra2019safetyofmobile pages 3-4, alexandra2019safetyofmobile pages 2-3):

1. **System limits definition:** usage, spatial, temporal, and other limits, including the entire mobile platform, robot arm, end-effectors, surrounding roads, work areas, human interaction, and interfering factory traffic.
2. **Hazard identification:** mechanical (crush, impact, shear, entanglement), electrical, thermal, noise, chemical (coolant, cleaning solvents), and radiation (if laser testing is performed) hazards.
3. **Representative contact scenarios:** transient and quasi-static collisions between the mobile manipulator and personnel at every reachable position and speed, including during transit, docking, and manipulation.
4. **Combined-system hazards:** The mobile base, manipulator, payload, sensors, and actuators must be assessed as an integrated system, not as separate components (alexandra2019safetyofmobile pages 3-4, alexandra2019safetyofmobile pages 2-3).
5. **Risk evaluation and reduction:** inherently safe design, safety-rated functions (monitored stop, speed limiting, force limiting), protective measures (sensors, interlocks, barriers where needed), and residual-risk documentation.
6. **Validation:** stopping-performance tests, force/pressure measurements against ISO/TS 15066 limits, interlock verification, speed-and-separation tests, and documented acceptance (valori2021validatingsafetyin pages 5-6, scibilia2021analysisofinterlaboratory pages 1-2, scibilia2021analysisofinterlaboratory pages 2-3).

For a university shop where people move freely, the most practical collaborative mode is **PFL during manipulation** (UR12e's built-in force/torque sensing supports this) combined with **SSM during transit** (MiR250's laser scanners provide separation monitoring). However, PFL speed limits of 0.12 m/s worst-case would impose severe cycle-time penalties if people are routinely nearby; zoning the shop to separate transit corridors from active workstations is strongly recommended.

---

## 5. Commissioning Effort vs. Manual Build

The following table provides estimated person-hours for commissioning the mobile-manipulator cell compared with building the machine manually. These are author estimates informed by published evidence, as no source reports this exact application.

| Activity | Mobile-Manipulator Cell (person-hours estimate) | Manual Build (person-hours estimate) | Notes/Source |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Mechanical hardware setup: MiR–UR mounting, cabling, docking stations | 60–120 | 0–8 | **Author’s estimate.** Includes two mobile platforms, arm mounts, utilities, tool racks, charging, docking or stabilization, and CNC interfaces. Integrated mobile manipulators require system-level treatment rather than separate arm/base integration (vitolo2022mobilerobotsand pages 5-6, alexandra2019safetyofmobile pages 2-3). |
| Safety risk assessment and documentation | 80–160 | 8–24 | **Author’s estimate.** Mobile manipulation, CNC access, sharp tools, suspended loads, collaborative contact, and shop traffic require an iterative ISO 12100 and ISO 10218 assessment; manual work still needs ordinary shop controls (mariano2026roboticsafetyin pages 3-3, faria2020safetyrequirementsfor pages 4-6, duplak2025applicationofsafety pages 2-4). |
| Station registration and accuracy validation | 40–80 | 0 | **Author’s estimate.** Covers AprilTag and hand–eye calibration, datum probing, error budgets, repeated docking trials, and acceptance limits. Examples range from 50–100 mm error with SLAM alone to 10 mm or less with fiducials, 0.19 mm vision-compensated offset, and ±0.12 mm after structured station calibration (hifi2025flexibleandintelligent pages 69-74, hifi2025flexibleandintelligent pages 74-80). |
| Gripper and end-effector design and fabrication | 200–400 | 24–60 | **Author’s estimate.** Robot scope includes part grippers, vacuum tooling, nutrunners, O-ring tools, compliant insertion tools, tool changing, sensing, and storage. Custom fixtures and grippers are major reintegration burdens (messina2024researchopportunitiesfor pages 39-42, messina2024researchopportunitiesfor pages 28-30). |

Published mobile machine tending remains predominantly prototype or conceptual (feiyu2024anintelligentframework pages 43-47, feiyu2024anintelligentframework pages 61-65). |

Minute-scale programming applies to simple cobot screwdriving, not complete integration and recovery behavior (brera2022collaborativescrewdrivingintegrating pages 35-38, brera2022collaborativescrewdrivingintegratinga pages 35-38). |

| **Total commissioning before the first machine** | **1,230–2,470** | **140–340** | **Author’s estimate obtained by summing the rows above.** No published benchmark exists for this exact cell. General three-dimensional deformable-object routing remains unresolved (caporali2026roboticperceptionand pages 24-25, caporali2026roboticperceptionand pages 23-24, govoni2026designcontroland pages 31-34). |

The ranges are author estimates informed by published deployment, calibration, safety, and programming evidence because no source reports this exact application.*

### 5.1 Key Findings

**For a single machine, the commissioning-to-build ratio is approximately 3:1 to 7:1 against automation.** The estimated total to produce one machine via the mobile-manipulator cell is 1,430–2,850 person-hours, versus 360–740 person-hours for a fully manual build. The dominant cost is commissioning: approximately 1,230–2,470 person-hours for end-effector design, assembly programming (~90 steps at 3–7 hours each), vision and sensor commissioning, safety assessment, process validation, and debugging. By comparison, cobots claim minute-scale programming for individual simple tasks, but complete cell integration is orders of magnitude larger (brera2022collaborativescrewdrivingintegrating pages 35-38).

**In calendar time,** assuming a team of two robotics-capable graduate students working approximately 30 productive hours per week, commissioning would take approximately 20–40 weeks (5–10 months). The manual build by an experienced instrument maker or machinist might take 10–20 weeks of elapsed time. Conventional automation deployment is reported at 8–17 weeks, but that assumes a production-ready integrator and a repeating task (brera2022collaborativescrewdrivingintegrating pages 35-38).

**The break-even point for the robotic cell** depends on reuse. If the same programs, grippers, and processes are used for 5–10 identical machines, the per-unit commissioning amortization drops to 120–500 person-hours, approaching parity with manual build. However, the question specifies a one-off machine, making the economic case clearly unfavorable unless the cell commissioning itself is a research objective.

### 5.2 Recommendation

For a one-off desktop LPBF machine in a university shop, **building manually with selective cobot assistance** is more practical than fully commissioning the mobile-manipulator cell. A pragmatic hybrid approach would:

1. **Build the first machine primarily by hand**, using the UR12e arms on their MiR250 bases as general-purpose material handlers and CNC tending assistants for the longest-running machining operations.
2. **Automate 2–3 high-value repetitive subtasks** (e.g., CNC part loading/unloading during long mill runs, kit transfer between stations, ultrasonic wash loading) where the programming effort is modest and the time saved during machining is substantial.
3. **Treat the remaining assembly as a development testbed**: program and validate individual skills (screw driving, dowel insertion, O-ring installation with custom tooling) on representative sub-assemblies, building toward a future production capability.
4. **Retain people for all tasks on the person-only list plus the additions identified in Section 2.1**, and do not attempt dual-mobile-base coordinated lifting.

This approach produces the machine in approximately 400–700 person-hours while building reusable robotic skills that could be deployed if a second or third machine is built, and avoids the 1,200–2,500 person-hour commissioning overhead for a cell that runs once.

# Critical Review: Two Mobile Manipulators Building a Desktop LPBF Machine in a University Shop

## 1. Published Examples and Industrial Practice of Mobile Manipulators for CNC Machine Tending and Assembly

### 1.1 Maturity of Mobile-Manipulator Machine Tending

Autonomous mobile manipulators (AMMs) combining an AMR base with a cobot arm are recognized as a scalable solution for high-mix, low-volume CNC tending, but the published evidence base remains largely at the prototype or conceptual level (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000003). A systematic review of robotic machine-tending literature found that AMM-based loading and unloading using 3D point-cloud object detection, marker recognition, and CNN-based material handling are classified as prototypes, with no fully autonomous system yet replacing a human for tasks such as cycle start, emergency handling, or screen-based machine interaction (pqac-00000002). One cited example uses a KUKA AMR with a gripper and vision on the end-effector to pick raw material from local storage and transport it to a machine for loading, but this remains a demonstration rather than a production deployment (pqac-00000038).

### 1.2 Achieved Positioning Accuracy After Docking and Re-Registration

Positioning accuracy is the principal bottleneck for mobile manipulation. SLAM-only AMR navigation produces positioning errors of approximately 50–100 mm (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000035). Adding fiducial markers (ARTags) together with a wrist-mounted vision system reduces errors to 10 mm or less, representing an improvement of more than 80% (pqac-00000000). Vision-based compensation in one study achieved an average offset of 0.19 mm (pqac-00000035). In a robotic-chemist application where a touch-sensitive six-point station calibration was used, positioning accuracy improved to ±0.12 mm with ±0.005° orientation over 563 movements (pqac-00000034). The KUKA KMR iiwa has a manufacturer-quoted positioning accuracy of up to ±5 mm, with experimental results at low speed generally remaining below 2 mm (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000037). Your proposed ±3 mm AMR docking plus AprilTag re-registration with a wrist camera is therefore realistic and consistent with published results, provided that station-specific datum probing or touch-off is added as a secondary verification. For CNC loading at ±0.1 mm repeatability, the cobot's own repeatability (±0.05 mm for UR10e/12e) must be used relative to a station-registered frame, not the AMR pose.

### 1.3 Uptime, Failure Rates, and Cycle-Time Penalties

No published study reports operational uptime, mean-time-between-failure, or quantified cycle-time penalties for a mobile manipulator tending CNC machines in production. NIST's survey of manufacturing robotics barriers identified organizational uptime targets of 16,000–80,000 hours and noted that uncertainty about robotic reliability is a major adoption barrier (pqac-00000044). The docking overhead per station visit—including navigation, docking, registration verification, and tool change—is an inherent cycle-time penalty, estimated at 1–3 minutes per station visit based on AMR transit speeds and typical registration sequences, which is significant for short machining cycles but negligible for multi-hour CNC operations.

### 1.4 Commissioning Effort Per New Task

Cobot manufacturers claim that a simple screwdriving or pick-and-place task can be programmed in minutes, while conventional automation deployment commonly takes 8–17 weeks (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000042, pqac-00000043). However, full cell commissioning—including safety assessment, sensing, grippers, recovery logic, and validation—is substantially longer and is not well-quantified in the literature. In one case study of cobot welding for an SME, only about 3% of technically suitable welding jobs were actually automated because programming time was burdensome for small batches, even though 95% of jobs were theoretically feasible (pqac-00000032). NIST identifies long integration timelines, programming burden, and limited redeployability as persistent barriers to manufacturing robot adoption, particularly in high-mix production (pqac-00000044, pqac-00000045, pqac-00000046, pqac-00000050).

### 1.5 What Still Needs People

Published reviews consistently identify the following as requiring human involvement: emergency handling and machine-screen interaction for CNC cycle control (pqac-00000002); first-article verification, CAM programming, and tool setting; heavy-part handling beyond cobot payload; deformable-object manipulation (cables, hoses); exception handling and fault recovery; inspection requiring judgment; and process changes or new part introductions (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000051).

---

Your person-only list is **mostly correct but slightly too short**. The following items should be added or reconsidered:

**Items correctly kept manual:**
- Loading the 34.7 kg plate (exceeds payload)
- CAM and first-article runs
- Tool setting
- TIG welding thin-wall 316L
- Reading bore and height gauges (for one-off)

- Lifting anything over combined payload (84 kg module)

**Items that should be added to the person-only or person-shared list:**
- **F-theta lens installation (M85 thread):** The f-theta lens is an expensive, fragile optic on a large fine thread. Cross-threading risk, contamination risk, and uncertain thread engagement make robotic installation inadvisable for one unit.

For a university shop, the safer approach is to use a rated lifting device (vacuum lifter, hoist, or jib crane) for any part above approximately 10 kg and reserve dual-arm coordination for holding and orienting lighter components.

Torque-only inference is uncertain because friction can cause errors approaching 50% (pqac-00000008). | Use compatible fastener grades/coatings, approved anti-seize or pre-applied lubricant, clean threads and slow driving speed. *Table: Key failure modes for the proposed mobile-manipulator machining and assembly cell, with practical detection and mitigation controls. Severity reflects potential damage to personnel, machines, high-value components, or latent product quality.*

### 3.1 Detailed Discussion of Key Failure Modes

**Cross-threading and galling of stainless screws** are the highest-consequence assembly failures. Cross-threading occurs when external and internal threads engage on misaligned helices (pqac-00000041). Detection relies on torque–angle monitoring: each successful screw insertion produces a characteristic torque–angle signature, and deviations outside a taught window indicate faults. Torque-rate monitoring samples torque after each angular increment and compares the current deviation against a tolerance zone (pqac-00000040). Published general fault-recognition rates reach approximately 90–97% using teach-based, ANN, or ML classifiers, but deployment-ready performance on actual assembly lines remains an ongoing challenge (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000026). Torque-only control can deviate by up to 50% due to friction, making it unsuitable for precise fault detection without supplementary angle data (pqac-00000008).

Galling is a specific risk for stainless steel that is **not addressed in the robotic assembly literature**. It requires process-level mitigation: compatible alloy grades, anti-seize lubricant, clean threads, slow driving speed, and conservative torque limits. The torque signature for galling—a sudden, irregular torque increase with stick-slip behavior—overlaps with other friction anomalies, making automated detection unreliable without validated process-specific envelopes.

**Chips and coolant contamination** of fixtures and datums is the most common CNC machine-tending failure mode. Swarf on a vise jaw or chuck datum creates a seating error that propagates through machining. Detection requires dedicated close-up vision of datum surfaces, air-pressure/flow confirmation, and force-displacement monitoring during part seating.

**Part pose errors** from gripper misalignment or incorrect orientation cause downstream failures in CNC loading and assembly. Force/torque data during insertion show distinctive profiles—sawtooth patterns during successful threading, and distinctive force spikes or stalls during failures—but relating force/torque data to part geometry is identified as a missing capability (pqac-00000025).

**O-ring twist and incomplete seating** are especially dangerous for half-dovetail and internal rod glands where the groove is occluded. Force alone does not prove correct circumferential seating, and visual inspection may be inadequate for internal grooves. Full-circumference machine vision, borescope inspection, or pressure-decay testing after closure are the most reliable detection methods.

---

## 4. Safety Standards and Risk Assessment Requirements

### 4.1 Applicable Standards

The safety framework for your proposed cell must combine multiple standards because no single standard covers integrated mobile manipulators (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016):

- **ISO 10218-1:2025** addresses robot design and construction, including functional safety, operating modes, emergency stops, and speed limiting (pqac-00000011).
- **ISO 10218-2:2025** addresses robot system integration, covering cell layout, safeguarding, commissioning, programming, operation, and maintenance. The 2025 revision gives greater attention to collaborative applications (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000013).
- **ISO/TS 15066:2016** supplements ISO 10218 for collaborative operation and defines four modes: Safety-rated Monitored Stop (SRMS), Hand-Guiding (HG), Speed and Separation Monitoring (SSM), and Power and Force Limiting (PFL) (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000013, pqac-00000014). PFL requires that contact forces remain below body-region-specific thresholds. For a mobile manipulator where contact with the face cannot be excluded, the worst-case transient force limit is 65 N and the corresponding maximum interface speed is 0.12 m/s (pqac-00000052). The body model contains 29 specific contact locations grouped into 12 body regions; quasi-static limits are half the transient limits (pqac-00000053, pqac-00000054).
- **ISO 3691-4** addresses safety requirements for driverless industrial trucks, including AMRs (pqac-00000016).
- **ANSI/RIA R15.08** was developed specifically for industrial mobile robots and mobile manipulators to address gaps among AGV, AMR, and mobile-manipulator standards. At the time of key publications, it was announced for publication in early 2019 as a draft (pqac-00000012). It is now published and addresses the combined hazards of mobility and manipulation.
- **ISO 12100** provides the overarching risk-assessment methodology (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000014).

### 4.2 Risk Assessment Requirements for This Cell

A documented, iterative risk assessment is required covering (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000016):

1. **System limits definition:** usage, spatial, temporal, and other limits, including the entire mobile platform, robot arm, end-effectors, surrounding roads, work areas, human interaction, and interfering factory traffic.
2. **Hazard identification:** mechanical (crush, impact, shear, entanglement), electrical, thermal, noise, chemical (coolant, cleaning solvents), and radiation (if laser testing is performed) hazards.
3. **Representative contact scenarios:** transient and quasi-static collisions between the mobile manipulator and personnel at every reachable position and speed, including during transit, docking, and manipulation.
4. **Combined-system hazards:** The mobile base, manipulator, payload, sensors, and actuators must be assessed as an integrated system, not as separate components (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000016).
5. **Risk evaluation and reduction:** inherently safe design, safety-rated functions (monitored stop, speed limiting, force limiting), protective measures (sensors, interlocks, barriers where needed), and residual-risk documentation.
6. **Validation:** stopping-performance tests, force/pressure measurements against ISO/TS 15066 limits, interlock verification, speed-and-separation tests, and documented acceptance (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000053, pqac-00000054).

For a university shop where people move freely, the most practical collaborative mode is **PFL during manipulation** (UR12e's built-in force/torque sensing supports this) combined with **SSM during transit** (MiR250's laser scanners provide separation monitoring). However, PFL speed limits of 0.12 m/s worst-case would impose severe cycle-time penalties if people are routinely nearby; zoning the shop to separate transit corridors from active workstations is strongly recommended.

---

The ranges are author estimates informed by published deployment, calibration, safety, and programming evidence because no source reports this exact application.*

### 5.1 Key Findings

**For a single machine, the commissioning-to-build ratio is approximately 3:1 to 7:1 against automation.** The estimated total to produce one machine via the mobile-manipulator cell is 1,430–2,850 person-hours, versus 360–740 person-hours for a fully manual build. The dominant cost is commissioning: approximately 1,230–2,470 person-hours for end-effector design, assembly programming (~90 steps at 3–7 hours each), vision and sensor commissioning, safety assessment, process validation, and debugging. By comparison, cobots claim minute-scale programming for individual simple tasks, but complete cell integration is orders of magnitude larger (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000042).

**In calendar time,** assuming a team of two robotics-capable graduate students working approximately 30 productive hours per week, commissioning would take approximately 20–40 weeks (5–10 months). The manual build by an experienced instrument maker or machinist might take 10–20 weeks of elapsed time. Conventional automation deployment is reported at 8–17 weeks, but that assumes a production-ready integrator and a repeating task (pqac-00000042).

**The break-even point for the robotic cell** depends on reuse. If the same programs, grippers, and processes are used for 5–10 identical machines, the per-unit commissioning amortization drops to 120–500 person-hours, approaching parity with manual build. However, the question specifies a one-off machine, making the economic case clearly unfavorable unless the cell commissioning itself is a research objective.

### 5.2 Recommendation

For a one-off desktop LPBF machine in a university shop, **building manually with selective cobot assistance** is more practical than fully commissioning the mobile-manipulator cell. A pragmatic hybrid approach would:

1. **Build the first machine primarily by hand**, using the UR12e arms on their MiR250 bases as general-purpose material handlers and CNC tending assistants for the longest-running machining operations.
2. **Automate 2–3 high-value repetitive subtasks** (e.g., CNC part loading/unloading during long mill runs, kit transfer between stations, ultrasonic wash loading) where the programming effort is modest and the time saved during machining is substantial.
3. **Treat the remaining assembly as a development testbed**: program and validate individual skills (screw driving, dowel insertion, O-ring installation with custom tooling) on representative sub-assemblies, building toward a future production capability.
4. **Retain people for all tasks on the person-only list plus the additions identified in Section 2.1**, and do not attempt dual-mobile-base coordinated lifting.

This approach produces the machine in approximately 400–700 person-hours while building reusable robotic skills that could be deployed if a second or third machine is built, and avoids the 1,200–2,500 person-hour commissioning overhead for a cell that runs once.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides general background on machine tending but does not report published examples or industrial deployments specifically involving mobile manipulators tending CNC machines. It defines machine tending as operating and supervising machine tools, including loading and unloading workpieces, starting and stopping machines, adjusting settings, and inspecting output quality. These activities are characterized as repetitive, physically demanding, monotonous, and time-intensive. The text describes conventional industrial robotic machine-tending systems as improving productivity, reducing manual labor, increasing consistency, and improving operational efficiency. However, it states that conventional robots are generally task-specific and have limited adaptability when conditions or tasks change, often requiring substantial reprogramming or physical adjustment. It also notes that they typically operate in confined areas or cages and lack sufficient intelligence for safe human collaboration. No quantitative data are given in this excerpt for uptime, failure rates, cycle-time penalties, commissioning effort per new task, or the proportion of work still requiring human operators. The excerpt does indicate that humans may be relieved to focus on more complex tasks requiring critical thinking and decision-making, while machine tending itself includes monitoring, adjustment, and quality inspection functions.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes collaborative robots as suitable for repetitive and tedious screwdriving work, with the aim of reducing operator fatigue, monotony, and physical demand while improving productivity and flexibility. The reported workcell combines a cobot and a human operator working simultaneously on the same workpiece. Its capabilities include intuitive programming, offline simulation through RoboDK, numerical analysis in MATLAB, optimization of screwdriving sequences to minimize cycle time, and vision-based detection of screw presence and operator hand presence. A Python orchestrator uses these detection results to coordinate cobot actions and incorporate the optimized sequence. The excerpt also identifies limitations: cobot deployment commonly relies on heuristic rather than mathematical task-assignment methods, and the study’s collaborative system depends on detection algorithms and a defined workcell configuration. However, this excerpt does not provide information about stainless-steel fastener galling prevention, cross-threading detection, or torque-monitoring strategies. It does not describe torque thresholds, torque-angle signatures, current-based monitoring, anomaly classification, thread-forming behavior, lubrication, speed control, or other specific methods for detecting or preventing these failure modes. Therefore, the passage supports general capabilities and limitations of collaborative screwdriving automation but cannot substantiate technical conclusions about cross-thread detection or galling prevention.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not directly discuss collaborative robots, robotic screw-driving capabilities, cross-threading detection, or stainless-steel fastener galling prevention. It does, however, describe sensor-based approaches that could support robotic fastening monitoring. Screw loading is normally multiaxial: assembly produces transverse forces associated with torsional loading, while operation can introduce bending and shear in addition to axial pretension. A DiaForce thin-film sensor washer measures preload through a piezoresistive layer and temperature through a chromium meander; pressure changes can indicate screw loosening. Its pressure areas are read sequentially through a multiplexer and 16-bit ADC. Other sensor-integrating screws, including SmartScrew, measure axial force only, and some designs require external wiring and amplification. The review concludes that most available sensor-integrated fasteners either provide only uniaxial pretension measurement or weaken the screw, limiting their ability to characterize the machine’s operating state. Consequently, the excerpt provides no specific torque-monitoring strategy for identifying cross-threading, such as torque-angle signatures, abnormal torque thresholds, or torque-gradient analysis. It also gives no method for preventing galling in stainless-steel fasteners. The relevant implication is that axial-force-only monitoring may be insufficient for detecting faults involving torsional or transverse loading.
contexts.question: What are the capabilities and limitations of collaborative robots for robotic screw driving, cross-threading detection, and stainless steel fastener galling prevention? What torque monitoring strategies detect cross-threading?

contexts.context: The excerpt describes capabilities relevant to robotic screw-driving and bolting, but it does not specifically discuss collaborative robots, cross-threading detection, or stainless-steel fastener galling prevention. The proposed robotic bolting framework provides accurate driving-torque control, active compliance throughout the operation, supervisory coordination, multimodal human–robot interaction, real-time system visualization, and transitions between automatic and manual control. These features are intended to improve fault detection, operator situational awareness, safety, and compliant execution. The broader literature discussion indicates that combining visual feedback with force/torque sensing can improve insertion accuracy and support fixtureless assembly, while impedance and force control improve safety and dependability compared with rigid motion control. However, automation remains limited by poor adaptability to environmental and geometric variations, and existing systems are characterized as lacking reliable autonomy and fault-management capabilities. The excerpt provides no specific torque signatures, thresholds, or monitoring algorithms for detecting cross-threading, and no methods for preventing galling in stainless-steel fasteners. Thus, it supports force/torque monitoring and compliance as general enabling strategies, but not a detailed answer about cross-threading detection or galling mitigation.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not specifically discuss collaborative robots, cross-threading detection, or prevention of galling in stainless-steel fasteners. It does, however, describe monitoring and control approaches relevant to detecting abnormal screw insertion. Torque-only control monitors driving torque but can deviate by up to 50% because of friction and other unmodeled parameters, making it less suitable for high-precision fault detection. Torque-angle monitoring measures both torque and rotation angle; torque control with angle monitoring can detect friction variations and is useful for fault detection, while angle control with torque monitoring aims to reduce tension scatter to within ±15%. Torque-rate control additionally measures torque gradient and is described as more accurate and repeatable than torque-angle control, although it is more complex and often unnecessary. For quality control, the excerpt describes a taught torque-angle fastening signature: insertion is considered successful when the measured curve remains within a predefined torque-angle window, while significant deviations indicate faults. This approach can identify abnormal fastening behavior but requires a separate teaching process for each production procedure and is therefore less adaptable. The source provides no evidence about robot capabilities or limitations, nor does it identify a specific strategy for stainless-steel galling prevention.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides useful general guidance for assessing a mobile-manipulator cell in a shared workspace, but it does not specifically address mobile manipulators, the 2025 revision of ISO 10218-2, or ANSI/RIA R15.08. ISO/TS 15066 is identified as the relevant collaborative-robotics specification for situations in which humans and robots share a workspace and may physically contact one another. It establishes permissible biomechanical force and pressure limits that vary by body region, contact type, and contact area; contact geometry, including sharp or blunt edges, also affects risk. Verification should consider possible contact scenarios and measure or calculate force and pressure across the robot’s positions and speeds, since a single universal speed or force value may not ensure safety throughout the workspace. ISO 12100 supplies the overarching risk-assessment process: define intended use and limitations, identify hazards throughout the life cycle, assess risks including foreseeable misuse, reduce risks using inherently safe design and technical protective measures, and warn or train operators regarding residual risks. ISO 10218-1 addresses robot-manufacturer requirements, while ISO 10218-2 addresses integrators and users, including cell layout, safety-feature placement, barriers, and safety systems. The process is iterative until the required safety level is achieved.

contexts.context: The excerpt characterizes robotic cable and hose routing as an emerging but incomplete capability. Existing systems address following deformable linear objects (DLOs), managing contacts with clips and pegs, routing through slots, and threading. Local execution generally depends on tactile or force sensing, while vision is used primarily for global planning. Robots can perform selected autonomous subtasks: learned visual policies have been demonstrated for slot insertion, tactile feedback can guide weaving through slots, and force-based control can regulate clipping and detect contact states. However, much of the state of the art still relies on scripted or heuristic motion primitives—such as sliding, grasping, reorienting, clipping, and weaving—that must be coordinated by a higher-level planner. Reinforcement learning and multimodal sensing show promise for more adaptive behavior, and model-predictive control with learned wire dynamics has also been explored. Key limitations include the dominance of 2D planar experiments, limited coverage of full 3D routing and dynamic harnessing, and continued reliance on specialized external sensing and preprogrammed behaviors. The cited literature covers plastic and elastic DLOs, but only a subset addresses threading or slot insertion, and the need to robustly coordinate perception, contact management, planning, and execution remains unresolved.

contexts.context: The excerpt presents robotic cable routing as an established but challenging assembly operation for deformable linear objects (DLOs), including relatively stiff cables with both ends constrained. The described state-of-the-art approach combines tactile sensing with motion primitives: the robot reconstructs the local and nearby future shape of a cable, grasps it, follows its three-dimensional contour, and inserts predefined cable sections into intermediate clips. Experiments reportedly validate these primitives on a single-arm robot using DLOs made from different materials and arranged in different configurations, with two cable-routing use cases. The approach demonstrates that robots can autonomously perform constrained clip-insertion routing under specific conditions. However, autonomy is not presented as general-purpose: clip poses and the required travel distance along the cable are assumed known, and tactile reconstruction requires the cable diameter to be smaller than half the sensor height. The broader manipulation experiments also identify failures during the final assembly phase, including excessive forces for stiff objects, safety stops, and incorrect cable positioning in grippers. This excerpt does not provide a comprehensive survey of routing through arbitrary channels, hoses, or optical fibers, nor does it establish performance across complex, unknown environments. It therefore supports feasibility for structured clip-based routing, while highlighting dependence on prior geometric knowledge, sensor suitability, object properties, and careful force management.

contexts.context: The excerpt characterizes robotic cable and hose routing as a distinct manipulation problem in which a deformable linear object (DLO) must be arranged along a target path while maintaining contact with fixtures, clips, jigs, pivots, holes, or eyelets. Threading is a higher-precision subtask involving insertion through designated openings, such as needle-like holes or industrial assemblies. Existing systems commonly use action-based planning with scripted or learned reusable motion primitives, including clipping and insertion, rather than fully general autonomous manipulation. The literature is organized around DLO following, contact management, routing-sequence parsing and planning, and threading. Tactile and force sensing are especially important for local execution: they provide feedback for grip adjustment, tension maintenance, sliding, and alignment. Vision is primarily used for global route planning. The NIST Assembly Task Board is emerging as a standardized benchmark for routing and supports reproducible comparisons, although it represents a simplified scenario. The excerpt indicates that autonomous routing is feasible for constrained clipping, following, and insertion scenarios, but robust general-purpose routing through arbitrary clips and channels remains an open research problem.

contexts.context: The excerpt frames robotic cable and hose routing as part of the broader, still-open problem of manipulating deformable objects. Cables, wires, ropes, and hoses are categorized as deformable linear objects (DLOs), while semi-deformable linear objects (SDLOs) include rigid components such as connectors at cable ends. These objects are widely used in electromechanical systems including vehicles, aircraft, and 3C products, where assembly commonly involves grasping, routing, clipping or fixing cables, and inserting plugs. The text indicates that these operations are traditionally performed manually and can involve poor ergonomic conditions. Unlike rigid objects, deformable objects have shapes defined by theoretically infinite degrees of freedom, large configuration spaces, and highly nonlinear deformation dynamics. Consequently, conventional modeling, planning, and control methods cannot be applied directly. The relevant state of the art therefore involves integrating perception, simulation, control, and mechanics, as well as developing reusable robotic skills for operations such as grasping, contour following, routing, clipping, and connector insertion. However, this excerpt does not provide experimental success rates, specific autonomous routing systems, or detailed evidence about routing through clips and channels. It supports the conclusion that autonomous cable, hose, and fiber routing remains technically challenging, especially in perception, shape representation, contact handling, and robust control.

contexts.context: The excerpt presents robotic cable routing as an active but incomplete state of the art, focused primarily on deformable linear objects such as wiring harnesses. Existing research combines global vision with task-specific sensing and manipulation: tactile fingers support contour following and routing, tactile grippers maintain contact while sliding along cables, and CAD-driven fixtures, snap-fit holders, and routing clips constrain cables along prescribed paths. A demonstrated dual-arm cell uses tactile and proximity sensors on one arm for grasping, connector insertion, and routing, while a second arm stabilizes the harness and performs spot taping; final vision inspection supports error detection and recovery. This indicates that robots can autonomously perform substantial portions of cable routing through clips and holders under controlled conditions, including grasping, insertion, path following, securing, and verification. However, the excerpt characterizes full autonomy as an unresolved goal rather than a broadly solved capability. The main limitations are cable deformability and elasticity, lightweight components, tight clearances, localized and low-magnitude contact forces, occlusion, reflections, variable lighting, and sensitivity to geometric variation. Vision degrades near the end-effector, while wrist force/torque sensors may approach their noise floor. Existing systems are often isolated solutions for sensing, routing, insertion, or taping, rather than integrated, reconfigurable systems able to handle varied cables, hoses, or fibers and recover robustly from errors.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies misalignment during the preliminary spiral insertion as the principal failure mode for robotic nut/screw-like insertion. Friction caused by the stud’s raised lip and by the threads can make the nut stick, prevent recovery from misalignment, or cause the part to hang insecurely and fall when released. A final downward push can help align a mostly aligned nut, and the authors report no observed cross-threading in their trials; therefore, the excerpt does not provide a demonstrated torque-angle method for detecting cross-threading. During successful threading, forces have a saw-tooth profile, while the final downward motion produces a descending staircase in Z-force. Torque-based stopping can also generate false positives: gripper contact with the base plate may create enough frictional torque to satisfy the stopping criterion even though the intended threading condition is not necessarily complete. The authors propose detecting failures from distinctive force/torque profiles and time distributions, potentially aborting actions early and triggering recovery actions such as regrasping or restarting localization. They emphasize that estimating the held part’s pose and relating force-torque data to part geometry is a missing capability. The excerpt contains no discussion of stainless-steel galling, stripped threads, or explicit detection of incorrect seating beyond force/torque patterns and stopping criteria.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not directly describe robotic screw-insertion failure modes, torque-angle monitoring, or robot-specific detection algorithms for cross-threading, stripped threads, or incorrect seating. It does provide limited background on sensor-integrating fasteners that could support such detection. The DiaForce system uses a piezoresistive sensor layer in an instrumented washer to measure preload force, while a chromium meander measures temperature. Changes in pressure measured by the sensor layer indicate screw loosening. Other systems, including SmartScrew, measure axial force using a strain gauge integrated into the thread and transmit data to external electronics. contexts.context: The excerpt identifies self-tapping screw failures and problems during screw acquisition and alignment as common robotic screw-insertion fault scenarios. It describes a teach-method approach in which each successful insertion has a characteristic torque-angle fastening signature. The robot or control system compares the measured torque-angle curve with the taught trajectory and predefined torque-angle window; significant deviations are treated as indications of a fault. Torque-angle monitoring is also presented as useful for detecting friction variations and supporting fault detection, while angle control with torque monitoring can reduce tension scatter. However, the excerpt does not specifically explain how cross-threading is distinguished from other faults, nor does it provide dedicated detection criteria for stripped threads, incorrect seating, or galling of stainless-steel screws. Those conditions might manifest as deviations in torque, angle, or the overall fastening signature, but that inference is not explicitly stated in the provided text. contexts.context: The excerpt does not provide CNC machine-tending-specific results for cycle-time penalties from mobile-robot docking, uptime, or a direct repeatability figure. It describes mobile manipulators as combining a mobile platform with an onboard multi-axis arm and identifies their potential to bring inspection or other processes to the part, improving flexibility and reducing the need to move components to fixed cells. Their principal limitations are uncertain accuracy and repeatability, sensitivity to floor-surface conditions and wheel wear, reach and positioning variability, implementation cost, safety requirements, and the additional degrees of freedom introduced by platform motion. External sensing substantially improves positioning: vision-based compensation achieved an average offset of 0.19 mm, while relying only on SLAM produced 50–100 mm positioning errors; adding ARTags and vision reduced these errors to 10 mm or less. Thus, the excerpt supports improved localization through integrated vision but does not establish CNC tending performance, docking time overhead relative to a fixed robot, achieved arm repeatability, or system uptime. Those requested metrics would need to be obtained from another section or source.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes autonomous mobile manipulators (AMMs) as combinations of collaborative robots and autonomous mobile robots. For CNC or other machine-tending applications, they can transport workpieces between machines or workstations and perform loading, unloading, picking, placing, and inspection. Sensors such as LIDAR, cameras, and end-effector cameras support environmental perception, obstacle avoidance, manipulation, and more complex operations. With AI, AMMs can adapt to dynamic environments, make decisions from real-time data, learn from their surroundings, and operate with reduced human intervention. contexts.context: The excerpt describes a general capability for detecting screwdriving faults through torque-angle signature monitoring, but it does not specifically identify cross-threading, stainless-steel fasteners, or a cross-threading prevention method. In the taught-signature approach, each successful screw insertion is expected to generate a characteristic torque-angle curve. contexts.context: The excerpt describes cross-threading as an abnormal jointing condition caused or revealed by uncertainty in the sensors and mechanical system. In robotic tightening, detection is based primarily on monitoring torque and/or rotational angle during operation. For high-accuracy applications, the reported method is torque-rate monitoring: torque is sampled after each specified angular increment, and the current torque-rate deviation is compared with a tolerance zone derived from the desired torque/angle curve. A deviation outside that zone is used to identify abnormal tightening behavior, which can include cross-threading, jamming, or slippage. Automatic tightening devices may also provide false-torque detection, self-diagnosis, and alarm outputs based on torque/angle sensor feedback. However, the excerpt does not give a detailed torque-angle waveform or explicit numerical signature that uniquely distinguishes cross-threading from normal thread engagement. It also does not report a specific cross-threading detection accuracy, detection rate, sampling rate, or false-alarm rate. It cautions that torque/angle sensing data can be unstable because of the dynamic tightening process, motivating intelligent controllers for more reliable fault detection. The cited 10% torque-to-clamping-force conversion and 25–30% fit-torque range concern tightening process parameters, not cross-threading detection rates or signatures.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not discuss NIST research, provide typical industrial robot deployment times, or quantify programming effort for assigning robots new tasks. It does, however, identify several cobot deployment and commissioning barriers. Integrating cobots into brownfield manufacturing environments is difficult because legacy equipment and software may be incompatible, requiring changes to physical layouts and production-management systems. These integration challenges can produce substantial downtime, higher costs, and a steep learning curve as operators adapt to new workflows. Economic barriers include high purchase and integration costs, uncertain long-term return on investment, and especially acute financial constraints for SMEs. Safety and compliance are also major concerns: cobots must meet rigorous and evolving standards such as ISO/TS 15066, while excessive safety restrictions may reduce promised productivity gains. Post-deployment commissioning requires continuous reassessment of safety mechanisms as workflows, infrastructure, and operator behavior change. The excerpt also notes that simplified, interactive end-user programming interfaces allow non-technical operators to configure and adjust cobot behavior in real time, potentially reducing dependence on engineers, but it gives no numerical estimate of programming time or effort. Overall, the cited material supports a qualitative account of integration, economic, safety, downtime, training, and usability challenges, not the requested NIST findings or industry benchmark figures.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes the ISO/TS 15066 framework for power-and-force-limited (PFL) collaborative robot applications, but it does not reproduce the numerical force and pressure values from Table 1. It states that the body model contains 29 specific contact locations grouped into 12 body regions, with each location assigned biomechanical maximum-force and maximum-pressure limits. The limits distinguish quasi-static (QS) contacts from transient impacts: for values applicable to QS contact, the corresponding transient-impact threshold is obtained by multiplying the value by two. Some limits apply only to transient contacts, and QS contact is prohibited for those locations. The excerpt also explains that these thresholds derive from research on pain-onset levels and are used to establish robot speed limits based on the effective moving mass and the body region involved. It discusses biofidelic sensors and impact testing for validating compliance. However, the excerpt provides no numerical ISO/TS 15066 limits, no complete body-region table values, and no information about the speed reduction required for mobile manipulators. Those details would need to be obtained from the cited standard, Table 1 in a readable form, or another source specifically addressing mobile-manipulator speed reduction.

contexts.context: The excerpt applies ISO/TS 15066 to autonomous mobile cobots operating in Power and Force Limiting (PFL) mode. It gives body-region maximum transient-contact forces and the corresponding calculated maximum interface speeds. The force limits are: skull/forehead 130 N, face 65 N, lower legs 260 N, thighs/knees 440 N, chest 280 N, abdomen 220 N, pelvis 360 N, upper arms 300 N, lower arms 320 N, and hands 280 N. The table also lists stiffness values and maximum speeds: 0.17 m/s for skull/forehead, 0.12 m/s for face, 0.216 m/s for lower legs, 0.401 m/s for thighs/knees, 0.408 m/s for chest and abdomen, 0.507 m/s for pelvis, 1.041 m/s for upper arms, 1.163 m/s for lower arms, and 1.331 m/s for hands. Because posture cannot be guaranteed, the authors include skull and face contacts and select the face value as the worst case, adopting 0.12 m/s as the safety speed limit. The excerpt does not provide ISO/TS 15066 pressure limits or a percentage speed-reduction requirement; it only supports limiting the mobile manipulator/interface to the stated worst-case speed.

Question: We are checking, in simulation, whether two collaborative robot arms (Universal Robots UR12e, the renamed UR10e: 12.5 kg payload including tooling, 1300 mm reach, built-in force/torque sensing), each on a MiR250 mobile base (docking to markers within about +-3 mm, then re-registering each station from an AprilTag with a wrist camera), could make and assemble a one-off desktop laser powder bed fusion machine in a university shop: unpacking deliveries, sawing bar, loading and unloading a Haas VF-4 vertical mill (with an HRT210 4th axis) and a Haas ST-10-class CNC lathe, deburring, ultrasonic washing, measuring, kitting parts onto a long table, then assembling about 90 steps: FKM O-rings in face glands, half-dovetail grooves and internal rod-gland grooves (with ring loaders, rollers and mandrels as end-of-arm tools), about 130 M3-M6 stainless screws driven with a nutrunner and an angle-head nutrunner, dowel pins, helical inserts, bearings, a ball screw and linear rail, cartridge heaters and thermocouples, optics (a galvo scan head, an f-theta lens on an M85 thread), and a final integration where a person with a hoist moves the 84 kg process module onto a storage-system tray. Our current plan keeps a person for: loading a 34.7 kg aluminium plate blank onto the mill with a vacuum tube lifter, CAM and first-article runs, tool setting, TIG welding a thin-wall 316L tube to flanges, reading bore and height gauges, routing hoses, fibres and cables, threading small fittings with tubes attached, installing a felt-and-PTFE bore seal, and lifting anything over the arms' combined payload.

Please review this plan critically, with sources: (1) published examples and industrial practice of mobile manipulators (AMR plus cobot) tending CNC machines and doing assembly in high-mix, low-volume or one-off settings: achieved positioning accuracy after docking and re-registration, uptime and failure rates, cycle-time penalties, commissioning effort per new task, and what still needed people; (2) which of the steps above are realistic for cobots today and which are not, and whether our person-only list is too long or too short (for example: can cobots route cables and hoses, install felt seals, TIG weld one-off parts, read bore gauges, thread fittings with tubing attached, handle 15-35 kg plates as a pair); (3) the hardest failure modes to expect (chips and coolant, fixture seating, part pose errors, cross-threading and galling of stainless screws, dropping parts, O-ring twist), and how they are detected; (4) safety for a shop where people and mobile manipulators work together: ISO 10218-1/-2 (2025), ISO/TS 15066, ANSI/A3 R15.08 for industrial mobile robots, and what a risk assessment for this cell would need; (5) a realistic estimate of the person-hours and calendar time to commission such a cell for one machine compared with simply building it by hand. Give concrete numbers where they exist and say clearly where you are estimating.

# Critical Review: Two Mobile Manipulators Building a Desktop LPBF Machine in a University Shop

## 1. Published Examples and Industrial Practice of Mobile Manipulators for CNC Machine Tending and Assembly

### 1.1 Maturity of Mobile-Manipulator Machine Tending

Autonomous mobile manipulators (AMMs) combining an AMR base with a cobot arm are recognized as a scalable solution for high-mix, low-volume CNC tending, but the published evidence base remains largely at the prototype or conceptual level (feiyu2024anintelligentframework pages 43-47, khishtan2026areviewof pages 2-4). A systematic review of robotic machine-tending literature found that AMM-based loading and unloading using 3D point-cloud object detection, marker recognition, and CNN-based material handling are classified as prototypes, with no fully autonomous system yet replacing a human for tasks such as cycle start, emergency handling, or screen-based machine interaction (feiyu2024anintelligentframework pages 43-47). One cited example uses a KUKA AMR with a gripper and vision on the end-effector to pick raw material from local storage and transport it to a machine for loading, but this remains a demonstration rather than a production deployment (feiyu2024anintelligentframework pages 43-47).

### 1.2 Achieved Positioning Accuracy After Docking and Re-Registration

Positioning accuracy is the principal bottleneck for mobile manipulation. SLAM-only AMR navigation produces positioning errors of approximately 50–100 mm (hifi2025flexibleandintelligent pages 74-80). Adding fiducial markers (ARTags) together with a wrist-mounted vision system reduces errors to 10 mm or less, representing an improvement of more than 80% (hifi2025flexibleandintelligent pages 74-80). Vision-based compensation in one study achieved an average offset of 0.19 mm (hifi2025flexibleandintelligent pages 74-80). In a robotic-chemist application where a touch-sensitive six-point station calibration was used, positioning accuracy improved to ±0.12 mm with ±0.005° orientation over 563 movements (hifi2025flexibleandintelligent pages 69-74). The KUKA KMR iiwa has a manufacturer-quoted positioning accuracy of up to ±5 mm, with experimental results at low speed generally remaining below 2 mm (hifi2025flexibleandintelligent pages 208-214, hifi2025flexibleandintelligent pages 63-69). Your proposed ±3 mm AMR docking plus AprilTag re-registration with a wrist camera is therefore realistic and consistent with published results, provided that station-specific datum probing or touch-off is added as a secondary verification. For CNC loading at ±0.1 mm repeatability, the cobot's own repeatability (±0.05 mm for UR10e/12e) must be used relative to a station-registered frame, not the AMR pose.

### 1.3 Uptime, Failure Rates, and Cycle-Time Penalties

No published study reports operational uptime, mean-time-between-failure, or quantified cycle-time penalties for a mobile manipulator tending CNC machines in production. NIST's survey of manufacturing robotics barriers identified organizational uptime targets of 16,000–80,000 hours and noted that uncertainty about robotic reliability is a major adoption barrier (messina2024researchopportunitiesfor pages 17-20). The docking overhead per station visit—including navigation, docking, registration verification, and tool change—is an inherent cycle-time penalty, estimated at 1–3 minutes per station visit based on AMR transit speeds and typical registration sequences, which is significant for short machining cycles but negligible for multi-hour CNC operations.

### 1.4 Commissioning Effort Per New Task

Cobot manufacturers claim that a simple screwdriving or pick-and-place task can be programmed in minutes, while conventional automation deployment commonly takes 8–17 weeks (brera2022collaborativescrewdrivingintegrating pages 35-38, brera2022collaborativescrewdrivingintegratinga pages 35-38). However, full cell commissioning—including safety assessment, sensing, grippers, recovery logic, and validation—is substantially longer and is not well-quantified in the literature. In one case study of cobot welding for an SME, only about 3% of technically suitable welding jobs were actually automated because programming time was burdensome for small batches, even though 95% of jobs were theoretically feasible (schumacher2022technologyadoptionof pages 5-7). NIST identifies long integration timelines, programming burden, and limited redeployability as persistent barriers to manufacturing robot adoption, particularly in high-mix production (messina2024researchopportunitiesfor pages 17-20, messina2024researchopportunitiesfor pages 34-37, messina2024researchopportunitiesfor pages 13-17, messina2024researchopportunitiesfor pages 20-25).

### 1.5 What Still Needs People

Published reviews consistently identify the following as requiring human involvement: emergency handling and machine-screen interaction for CNC cycle control (feiyu2024anintelligentframework pages 43-47); first-article verification, CAM programming, and tool setting; heavy-part handling beyond cobot payload; deformable-object manipulation (cables, hoses); exception handling and fault recovery; inspection requiring judgment; and process changes or new part introductions (messina2024researchopportunitiesfor pages 34-37, messina2024researchopportunitiesfor pages 28-30).
